# ccrc PR Lifecycle Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** every workspace session carries a PR control in its chat header; a
merged PR archives its workspace automatically and losslessly; an archived
workspace can be deleted only by a human tap carrying a fresh state
fingerprint that `ccd` re-proves on the box at the instant of deletion; and the
one existing unguarded one-tap delete (`ccd ws-rm` behind
`DELETE /api/sessions/:id/workspace`) stops existing.

**Architecture:** four boxes' worth of work in one branch, in strict dependency
order. `ccd` (bash, on the fleet host) gains eight verbs — `caps`, `pr-state`,
`pr-open`, `ws-archive`, `ws-restore`, `ws-audit`, `ws-reap`, `ws-attic` — and
is the ONLY place any irreversible guard is evaluated, because it is the box
that owns the files. The agent's `EXEC_WHITELIST` changes from
first-argument matching to argv-**prefix** matching so `['ws-reap','--expect']`
can be a machine-checked statement that ccrc cannot reap without a
confirmation token, and gains no `gh` key at all. The server builds every ccd
argv in exactly one module (`ccdargv.ts`), decides mergedness in exactly one
module (`prstate.ts`), and sweeps PR state on a third `FleetWatcher` lane
beside the 2 s pane poll and the 10 s task sweep. The PWA renders a keycap that
never performs an action on tap, a sheet that does, and a reap flow whose
confirmation IS the fingerprint.

**Tech Stack:** bash (ccd), TypeScript, React 19, Fastify, vitest,
@testing-library/react.

**Spec:** [`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-29-ccrc-pr-lifecycle-design.md`](../specs/2026-07-29-ccrc-pr-lifecycle-design.md)

## Global Constraints

### Every line number in this plan is a navigation aid. The quoted text is the address.

**Locate every edit site — in every task, in every file, `ccd` and TypeScript and
CSS alike — by the surrounding text this plan quotes, never by the line number
printed beside it.** A citation like `ccd:221` or `ProjectCard.tsx:146-158` exists
to get you to the right screenful in one jump. The *authority* is always the
quoted code: the `local common; common=$(…)` line, the `{!collapsed && (` block,
the `case "$state" in` ladder, the `it('…')` whose name the step gives you.
`grep -n` for it and edit what you find.

Therefore: **a citation that is off is expected, and is never a stop condition.**
Off by five, off by twenty, off by two hundred — search for the quoted text, edit
the site you find, and record the real number in your report. Stop and ask only
when the quoted text is **absent**, or **appears more than once**, or **says
something materially different** from what the plan claims about it. Those three
mean someone changed the code's *behaviour* under this plan and a human has to
decide. A number that merely moved is not one of them.

And never resolve a mismatch the other way. Editing line 221 because the plan said
221, when the line the plan quoted now lives at 229, is how a plan silently edits
the wrong statement — worse than stopping, because it looks like it worked.

This is not hypothetical and it is not confined to one package. Files already
known to have moved *while this plan was being written*:

### The exec-whitelist rule (verbatim, and non-negotiable)

There is **NO `gh` key** in `EXEC_WHITELIST`, in any form, including
`[['pr','view']]` and `[['api']]`. The host token carries the `repo` WRITE
scope and there is no second layer — no read-only credential, no cwd sandbox —
so any `gh` entry makes that list the sole control between the PWA and
`gh pr merge`. **`ws-rm` is removed from it**: it is the unguarded legacy verb
and the PWA must not be able to emit it. `clip` is removed: dead grant, no
server call site emits it. `ws-gc` is absent and must stay absent — `['ws-gc']`
would permit `--prune`.

### Guard placement (verbatim)

*Guards for reversible actions may live server-side; guards for irreversible
actions must live in `ccd`, on the box that owns the files, re-evaluated at the
instant of the action.* Archive's guards are server-side. Every reap guard is
in `ccd`.

### Archiving vs deletion (verbatim)

**Archiving is automatic. Deletion is NEVER automatic** — not on a timer, not
after a grace window, not "when we are sure". A deferred deletion is an
automatic deletion whose confirmation happened before the facts did. `ws-reap`
fires only from a confirmed tap carrying a fresh fingerprint.

### ccd rules

- ccd is bash with `set -uo pipefail` and deliberately **NO `set -e`**.
  Exit-code discipline matters: `local x=$(cmd)` returns `local`'s status,
  never `cmd`'s. Declare first, assign second wherever the status is read.
- **HOME is the ONLY test-isolation boundary for ccd.** `PROJECTS_ROOT` and
  `WORKTREES_ROOT` derive from `$HOME` and take NO env override. Never add one.
- **NEVER run `ccd ws-gc --prune` or any destructive ccd verb against the real
  host.** All ccd behaviour is exercised through the isolated-HOME harness in
  `server/test/ccdWsHelpers.ts` only.
- Every new `cmd_*` opens with strict positional assertions — fixed arity, no
  getopt loop, no `"$@"` passthrough into `gh` or `git`, no flag that takes a
  filesystem path, no force/override flag anywhere, and
  `[[ $id =~ ^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$ ]]` before any path is built from an id.
- **ccrc asks `$main`; `$workdir` is only ever a path git is asked about.** Every
  branch, ref, upstream and push in this plan is resolved with
  `git -C "$PROJECTS_ROOT/$project"`, and the worktree's identity comes from
  `_ws_wt_branch` / `_ws_common_dir` (`ccd:303-314`, `:284-289`) — git's own
  record — never from a command run inside the directory, which answers from
  whatever repository owns that path. Deviations 4 and 5. The one class of read
  that must be `-C "$workdir"` is the **tree** — `status --porcelain` and the
  ignored set in `_ws_reap_eval`'s Phase B, which are questions about that
  directory's contents — and those run only after both `_ws_wt_branch` and
  `_ws_common_dir` have said `$main`.
- Git revision operands are validated with `rev-parse --verify` and
  `--`-terminated **after** the revisions. Verified in this worktree:
  `git diff --quiet -- A B` exits **0** (the shas become pathspecs);
  `git diff --quiet A B --` exits **1**; `git merge-base --is-ancestor -- A B`
  is correct (0/1); an empty operand exits **128**.

### PWA rules

- The pwa tsconfig sets `noUncheckedIndexedAccess: true` and also `include`s
  `test/`. Indexing an array yields `T | undefined` — write code that
  typechecks under it (`arr[0]!` where the value provably cannot be undefined,
  otherwise a guard), and say which you did and why in your report. The server
  package does **not** set this flag.
- The pwa vitest config has **no `globals: true`**. Any test file that renders
  more than once needs an explicit
  `import { cleanup } from '@testing-library/react'` plus `afterEach(cleanup)`.
- **Never use `userEvent.click` on anything inside a vaul `Sheet`.** It crashes
  jsdom in `getTranslate` and makes vitest **exit non-zero while printing
  "passed"**. Use `fireEvent.click`. **Always check the real shell exit code of
  a vitest run** (`npx vitest run; echo "exit=$?"`) — never trust the printed
  summary alone.
- Use only CSS tokens that exist in `pwa/src/styles/tokens.css`. Every new
  colour pair goes in `pwa/design/contrast-check.mjs`; the gate must stay at
  ALL PASS.

### Out of scope, permanently (spec §7)

No merge/close/reopen/edit/review/comment verb. No automatic deletion at any
delay. No cleanup of `closed`-unmerged PRs. **No override anywhere** for
`sensitive-ignored`, `tree-differs`, `dirty-tree`, `unpushed-commits` or
`stashes-present` — no flag, no config file, no "Remove anyway". No `ws-gc`
from the PWA. No prompt injection as a mechanism for anything, and **no
GitHub-sourced string is ever placed in a prompt, an argv, or a shell.** No
editing the PR body on the phone. Nothing under `~/.claude*`, the `.ccrc/` line
in `info/exclude`, or `~/.cc-limits` is ever touched. No attic GC.

- Commit after each task with a real message (no `wip`, no `--no-verify`); the
  body explains WHY. Do not touch files outside the ones your task names. Do
  not run the doc server, deploy, or push.

is why they are here and not in commit bodies.
They are recorded in this document rather than only in commit bodies, because the
plan and the code are two implementations of one decision: each of them changes
a contract (a helper's exit status, an array's record shape, or the verb's
output shape) and each therefore has call sites in this document that had to
move with it.

**1. `assembleFleet` takes PR state as its EIGHTH parameter, not its seventh.**
The spec says seventh; the live signature (`fleet.ts:30-38`) is
`(io, cfg, tmux, now, pendingDialogs, statuslines, taskProgress)` — seven
already. `prStates` is appended as the eighth. Same threading, same reasoning
as `tasks`; only the ordinal in the spec was stale.

**2. `ccd pr-state` computes and persists `phase`; `prstate.ts` computes the
value that goes on the wire; a test pins the two equal.** The spec puts the
merge predicate in `prstate.ts` (§4.1) *and* requires `prPhase`/`prNumber`/
`prCheckedAt` persisted in the registry (§2). The server cannot write the
registry: the agent's write whitelist is `.cc-clips` only (`whitelist.ts:79-81`),
and widening it to `.cc-sessions` to persist a cache would hand the PWA write
access to every session's registry — a far larger grant than this feature
needs. So the box that reads GitHub writes the fields, and the predicate exists
twice: once in `ccd` (persistence) and once in `prstate.ts` (the wire), with a
cross-implementation agreement test over the whole fixture matrix
(Task 12, Steps 6-7). This is the codebase's existing precedent for a rule that
must live on both boxes — `_ws_least_loaded` vs `limits.ts` `projectHome`,
documented in `shared/api.ts:71-78`. `ws-archive` reads `$REG/$id.prnumber` for
its `archivedreason`, which is the second reason the field has to be on disk.

**3. `PrState.reason` gains a ninth member, `'merge-unproven'`.** The spec
enumerates the union verbatim (design §2, `reason: 'timeout'|…|'error'|null`) and
says nothing about which reason accompanies the gh-said-MERGED-with-a-failed-
conjunct phase, because §6's error table covers failed READS only and this is not
one — GitHub answered, and it said merged. Spending `'error'` on it (as an
earlier draft of this plan did) renders *"GitHub could not be read."* about a
read that worked, sending the reader to check `gh auth` over a `mergeCommit` the
API never named. It is also the one case where the two implementations of the
predicate could disagree invisibly: `ccd` persisted no reason at all for it while
`prstate.ts` answered `'error'`, and the agreement test pinned only `phase`. Both
sides now emit `'merge-unproven'` and the agreement test pins `reason` too.

**4. Phase A's branch read is `_ws_wt_branch`, not `rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD`
inside the worktree — which splits one refusal token in two and renames another.**
The spec spells A6 and A7 literally as
`git -C "$wt" rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD` (§5.3), and §6's row *"Registry branch
≠ worktree HEAD"* names the refusal `branch-drift`. This plan uses
`_ws_wt_branch "$main" "$workdir"` (`ccd:303-314`) instead, everywhere a branch
name is read.

The reason is `main`'s own, from the `ccrc/ws-rm-fix` merge: **`rev-parse` inside
a directory is not scoped to `$main`.** It answers from whatever repository owns
that DIRECTORY, and after a hand-deletion plus a stray `git init` that need not
be `$main` at all. Measured on git 2.43: with a stranger `git init`ed at the
workdir on `attacker/main`, the directory read answers `attacker/main` while
`$main`'s own worktree record still says `ws/quiet-basin`. The spec's A7 then
compares a stranger's HEAD with our registry and prints the stranger's branch
name in our refusal; A6 fires `detached-head` whenever the read merely *failed*,
including for a directory that is not a repository at all. `_ws_wt_branch` reads
`git -C "$main" worktree list --porcelain`, so it cannot leave `$main`, survives
the directory being gone, and follows a rename. **One rule for the file:** ws-rm
already reads its branch this way, and two different answers to "which branch is
this workspace on" in one file is how the next bug gets written.

The cost is three token changes, all of them here rather than discovered later:

| spec | this plan | why |
|---|---|---|
| — | `no-worktree-record` | `_ws_wt_branch` exit 1: `$main` holds no registration for that path. Newly *reachable* as its own state; the spec's A6 answered it `detached-head`, about a HEAD it had not read. |
| `detached-head` | `detached-head` (narrowed) | Now exactly what it says: git *recorded* a detached HEAD (empty name, exit 0). No longer reachable via a failed read. |
| `branch-drift` | `registry-branch-drift` | Both sides of the comparison are now RECORDS — ccrc's registry and git's registration — not a directory that wandered. The old name says the worktree drifted; what is detected is that two records disagree, and the refusal prints both, as §6 requires. |

`foreign-worktree` (A8) stays, and its *reason* changes rather than its token: it
was placed immediately after the branch read to contain a name that might have
come from another repository, and no name can any more. It is retained because
the **directory** is still read by Phase B and still handed to
`git worktree remove` by `_ws_reap_tail` — ccd:333-349's argument verbatim — and
because `registered` cannot decide it alone: the record outlives the directory,
and a `git init` at that path leaves the record reading healthy with no
`prunable` marker. It therefore moves from "right after the branch read" to
"immediately before Phase B", which is the first thing that touches the
directory. Nothing is dropped; the guard's justification is restated at the site.

Two things this deviation deliberately does **not** change. The registry stays
the source of the branch name reap *operates* on (`stashes`, `@{upstream}`, the
tip, the PR bind, the CAS delete) — §5.3's "registry first, worktree second" is
kept, because reap must be able to refuse `incomplete-registry` for want of a
name rather than proceed with a partial one; git's record is what is entitled to
*veto* it, after which the two are equal by construction. And the audit
manifest's `branch` field stays the registry's, with `headMatchesRegistry`
carrying the corroboration and `detail` carrying both names on a disagreement:
the manifest's job is to report what ccrc recorded and whether git agrees, and a
manifest that silently substituted git's answer would hide exactly the
divergence the refusal exists to surface.

**5. `pr-open` pushes from `$main`, not from `$workdir` — and corroborates the
registry's branch against git's worktree record before it pushes at all.** The
spec spells `cmd_pr_open`'s step 6 literally as
`git -C "$wt" push --set-upstream origin "refs/heads/$branch:refs/heads/$branch"`
(§3.1). This plan writes `git -C "$main" …`, with the same refspec, still never
`--force`, still with the branch from the registry.

This is deviation 4's rule applied to the one place in the design that **writes
to the network**, and it has to be stated separately because deviation 4 only
fixed the *name*: the name was already the registry's here and was already
correct. What was wrong was the **repository the ref resolves in**. `-C "$wt"`
answers from whatever repository owns that DIRECTORY. Measured on git 2.43, in a
throwaway fixture built exactly like the test harness: hand-delete the worktree
directory, `git init` a stranger there on the same branch name `ws/quiet-basin`
with one commit, and give it an `origin` pointing at our bare origin — which is
what a hand-made clone left at that path looks like — and
`git -C "$wt" push … refs/heads/ws/quiet-basin:refs/heads/ws/quiet-basin` moves
**our** ref on **our** origin to the **stranger's** commit, rc 0. `gh pr create
--head ws/quiet-basin` then opens, emails and CIs a PR over that commit, and
§3's own framing — *"outward-facing, irreversible in public; closing a PR later
does not unsend the notifications"* — is why this is closed here rather than left
to be discovered in review.

The branch corroboration alone does **not** close it, and the plan says so at
the test: `$main`'s record for a stranger-squatted path still reads healthy with
no `prunable` marker (the record's gitdir file now points at the stranger's own
`.git`), so it still answers `ws/quiet-basin` and the drift rung passes. What
closes it is *where the ref is resolved*. Verified in the same fixture, because
moving the push had to be shown not to break what the push is for:
`git -C "$main" push --set-upstream origin refs/heads/<b>:refs/heads/<b>` sends
the commits made in the linked worktree (they are in the shared object store —
the origin's ref lands on `$main`'s ref, byte for byte), and it writes
`branch.<b>.remote` / `branch.<b>.merge` into the **common** config, byte-
identical to the same push run inside the worktree, so `@{upstream}` resolves
from the worktree afterwards and `_ws_reap_eval`'s `no-upstream` refusal reads
what it expects. A deleted origin still fails locally and immediately from
`$main` — rc 128, git's own stderr — so Step 1's *"aborts before any gh call when
the push fails"* still holds: nothing is created.

The corroboration is kept anyway, ahead of the push, because `$main`'s record is
the only thing that ties the registry's name to this workspace: without it a
stale registry entry (a branch renamed outside ccd) makes `pr-open` push a branch
no workspace is on and open a PR for it. It reuses `_ws_wt_branch`'s three rungs
in refusal form, worded for this verb — no record, recorded-detached, and
registry-vs-record disagreement — which is the same ladder `cmd_ws_rm`
(ccd:380/:390/:402) and `_ws_reap_eval` walk. After this, `$workdir` in
`cmd_pr_open` is a **key into git's records and nothing else**: no git command in
the verb takes `-C "$workdir"`, and the shipped-source test bans that string
alongside `-F` and `"$@"`, because a behavioural test can only pin today's push.

One further spec divergence this makes explicit rather than introduces: §5.3's
B4 spells `git -C "$wt" rev-parse "@{upstream}"`, and `_ws_reap_eval` already
reads that from `$main` (`"$branch@{upstream}"`) for exactly the same reason.
The rule for the file is now one line long: **ccrc asks `$main`; `$workdir` is
only ever a path git is asked about.**

**6. `_ws_status` reads `idle` as an ALLOWLIST, not `busy` as a denylist — so
`shell` and every future status word refuse.** Task 2's Step 3 text (and the
first shipped `ccd:132`) was `[[ "$st" == busy ]] && { echo busy; return 0; };
echo idle` — it refused the literal string `busy` and mapped everything else to
`idle`. Measured in an isolated HOME with the pane alive: `{"status":"shell"}`
answered `idle` and `ws-archive` archived the workspace at exit 0.

`shell` is what Claude Code writes while a **Bash tool command** is running, and
this repo had already fixed this exact bug on the server side and documented it
at `server/src/livestate.ts:14-30` — *"`idle` is the ONLY value that reads as
idle and everything else is busy"*, with the flapping, the wrong badge and the
spurious "back to idle" push it cost. The plan reintroduced the reverted logic on
the destructive-adjacent side, where the price is higher: `_ws_status` is
consumed three times — `cmd_ws_archive`'s gate (lossless, costs a pane),
`_ws_reap_eval`'s Phase D1, and the reap RESUME path's Phase D1 guard. The last
two gate `git worktree remove`, so a workspace running `npm test` through the
Bash tool read `idle` and the reap would have deleted the tree out from under it
— precisely the loss the resume-path guard was added to prevent, defeated by the
helper it calls. §5.3's rule that every guard is evaluated *"on the box, at the
instant of deletion"* is not satisfied by a guard that answers `idle` for
`shell`.

Fixed at the helper, so all three call sites are corrected at once. The comment
claiming parity with `_auto_swap_check`'s gate was false in the same direction —
`ccd:1101` is `[[ "$st" == "idle" ]] || return 0`, an allowlist — and asserted the
very parity that would have made the code correct; it now describes the code.
Everything else about the gate was already fail-closed and stays that way: absent
file, unreadable file, missing `status` key, truncated JSON, uppercase `BUSY`,
pretty-printed JSON and a non-numeric pane pid all return non-zero. The two
refusal DETAILS in Tasks 5 and 6 said *"the session is mid-turn"*, which is no
longer what `busy` means, and are reworded above.

Four more corrections travel with it, all in Task 2's own text, because the
alternative is Tasks 5 and 6 requoting the originals:

- **`_ws_ignored_digest` returns non-zero when the set cannot be READ.** It
  hashed a silent empty stream, so `/no/such/dir`, a corrupt repo and an
  `index.lock` contention all answered `sha256("")` — identical to a workspace
  that ignores nothing. Task 6 compares a stored digest against a live one to
  prove gitignored content is unchanged, and a failure on either side
  manufactured the match. The signal comes from `PIPESTATUS[0]`, git's own
  status, because the pipeline's cannot: `grep '^!! '` exits 1 on a legitimately
  empty set, so the function already returned non-zero for the healthy case.
- **The archive manifest is validated before it is persisted.**
  `_ws_archive_manifest`'s exit status was discarded and every field inside it
  `2>/dev/null`-swallowed, with no `[[ -s ]]`, no parse and no guard before
  `_reg_set "$id" archived`. A workspace whose worktree had moved away archived
  at exit 0 with `dirty:0`, `worktreeBytes:0` and `ignoredDigest = sha256("")` —
  a record asserting a clean, empty tree — and a box without `python3` persisted
  syntactically invalid JSON as the archive record. That record is what Task 5's
  audit ladder and Task 6's reap compare against, so it is now a refusal naming
  the rung that failed.
- **The manifest's tree reads are entitled, not assumed.** `git -C "$workdir"
  status --porcelain` and the ignored set ran on the registry's word alone. They
  now run only after `_ws_wt_branch` and `_ws_common_dir` both say `$main` — the
  ordering Global Constraints prescribes and the pair `cmd_ws_rm` requires
  (`ccd:396-400`). This first landed with registry-vs-record branch drift
  refusing as well, on the argument that the manifest would otherwise file
  another branch's tip under this workspace. Deviation 7 corrects that half: the
  entitlement question is about the DIRECTORY, and drift is answered by recording
  both names instead.
- **`cmd_ws_archive`'s already-archived path `return`s instead of `exit`ing.**
  `ccd` is sourceable, so `exit 0` terminated an in-process batch caller at its
  first already-archived workspace and reported success — and the level-triggered
  sweep the idempotence exists for is exactly such a caller.

**7. The archive manifest RECORDS branch drift (`worktreeHead`, and a null
`tip`); it does not refuse on it.** Deviation 6's third bullet over-corrected.
Corroborating `$workdir`'s identity before reading its tree was right, and stays;
applying the same refusal to *which branch is checked out* was not. Three ordinary
states refused permanently, identically on retry, measured in an isolated HOME:
`git branch -m <new>` inside the worktree, `git checkout other-branch` to compare
something, `git checkout --detach` (what `git bisect` leaves) — all three
answering `cannot describe <id> truthfully — nothing was touched`, exit 1. A
fourth, detached *and* the registry's branch deleted by hand, refused twice over.

None of those makes a workspace undescribable: the directory is a genuine
worktree of `$main`, every field is readable, and the checked-out branch is a
FACT. Three things in the tree already said so. Task 2's Context makes the
identical argument for a dirty tree. `_ws_wt_branch`'s contract is that it
*follows a branch rename whether ccd or the user did it* (`ccd:377-383`). And
`cmd_ws_rm` — the verb that **deletes** — handles this very divergence by
proceeding with a note: *the registry is a witness, never the decider*
(`ccd:465-471`). The lossless verb had become stricter than the destructive one.

What makes it a defect rather than a preference is convergence. `ws-archive` is
the one verb here that runs with no human in the loop: Task 14's level-triggered
sweep fires it every 120 s and `archiveMerged` discards the exit code
(`if (!res.ok) continue`), so a refusal nothing can clear keeps the workspace in
the live fleet forever, re-logging the same line to ccd's stderr where no UI shows
it. `ccd ws-rename` — the supported path — keeps registry and record in sync and
archived fine, so the failure was confined to exactly the states ccd's own
comments say to follow rather than refuse.

The manifest therefore carries **`worktreeHead`**: git's own answer for the path,
beside the registry's claim in `branch`. It is the same fact Task 5 fingerprints
as `worktreeHead=` and puts on the wire as `headMatchesRegistry`, and `""` is
`_ws_wt_branch`'s answer for a recorded detached HEAD — the same `""` Task 5
compares against `$branch`. **`tip` becomes JSON `null`** when the branch the
registry names no longer resolves, which is what a hand-rename leaves behind;
never `""`, never a substitute oid, because filing the renamed branch's tip under
`branch` would be the forgery that rung existed to prevent. Every state now
recorded is one `ws-reap` refuses in its own right — `registry-branch-drift`,
`detached-head`, `branch-missing` — evaluated on the box at the instant of
deletion, which is where a refusal costs a deferred cleanup and nothing more.

The distinction is git's, not ours: measured on git 2.43, `rev-parse --verify
--quiet` exits **1** for an absent ref in a repository it can read and **128**
when it cannot read the repository at all (without `--quiet`, 128 for both). So
`tip` is a field when git answers and a refusal when it cannot be asked, and
`--quiet` is load-bearing rather than cosmetic. The rule this leaves for the whole
verb is stated in Task 2's Context, because the alternative is re-deciding it
per field: **archive refuses only what it cannot describe.**

**8. `_pr_py` takes its PROGRAM on fd 3, not on stdin — the plan's own form gave
the helper an empty stdin and made every PR in the fixture disappear.** Task 3's
Step 7 shipped `python3 - "$@" <<'PY'` with the header comment *"stdin = the gh
rows JSON"*. Both cannot be true: `-` tells python to read the program FROM
stdin, the heredoc IS stdin, and python consumes all of it as source. Measured
side by side in a throwaway shell, same script, same argv:

| form | `sys.argv[1:]` | `sys.stdin.read()` |
|---|---|---|
| `python3 - "$@" <<'PY'` | `['state','x']` | `''` |
| `python3 /dev/fd/3 "$@" 3<<'PY'` | `['state','x']` | `'[{"n":1}]'` |

So `rows_in()` answered `[]` for every call, `pick` chose nothing, and **every
fixture — merged, draft, closed, fork, unreachable — reported `phase:"none"` at
exit 0**: not a crash, an answer, and the one answer that means *"ready to open a
PR"*. Task 3's own tests caught it (8 red of 25 at Step 10, including `expected
'none' to be 'merged'`), which is the only reason it is a footnote rather than a
sweep lane that silently un-merged the fleet.

The rows cannot move to argv instead — §7 is that **no GitHub-sourced string is
ever placed in a prompt, an argv, or a shell** — so the program is what moves.
`sys.argv` is identical either way, so the `sys.argv[2:14]` unpack and every
call site are unchanged; the heredoc body is byte-identical. Task 5 adds mode
`pick` to this same helper and inherits the fix.

**9. A sweep that writes `prphase=none` (or `no-commits`) CLEARS `prnumber`.**
Step 7 wrote `if number is not None: put('prnumber', number)` — the number was
never written for a phase that has none, and never removed either. Phase and
number are one answer, so persisting half of it is a lie with two named
consumers: `fleet.ts` builds `{phase: r.prPhase ?? 'unchecked', number:
r.prNumber}` straight from the two registry fields, so a deleted PR renders
`#42` under a cap whose own copy is *"no pull request yet"*; and `cmd_ws_archive`
reads `$REG/$id.prnumber` for `archivedreason`, filing `merged:#42` for a PR that
no longer binds. It is not hypothetical for a long-lived box: a PR can be
deleted, force-pushed out of reachability, or have its 144-slug branch name
recycled by `ws-reap` while the number stays on disk from the last good read.

The field is **removed, not blanked**, so it is absent exactly as it is for a
workspace that never had one (`numOrNull` and `[[ =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]` treat the two
alike today; the file's absence keeps them alike for a reader that checks `-f`).
A failed read cannot clear a number, on either of its two guards: an exit-code
failure returns from `_gh_pr_list` before `_pr_py` is called, and an rc-0 body
that does not parse as a list makes `rows_in` answer `None`, which emits the
id-less `unknown/error` object and exits before any `put`/`clear` (the
single-guard version of this claim was disproved by the Task 3 review's finding
1 — an unintelligible rc-0 body walked straight into the clear path). Both are
pinned by `leaves the persisted prphase untouched`. Raised as Task 1
review finding 3, carried in the execution ledger, and implemented here because
Task 3 is the only writer.

**10. `pr-state`'s local facts — `tip`, `ahead`, `dirty` — are measurements or
JSON `null`, never a fabricated zero; and proof 0 skips its ancestry rung when
there is no tip to reach from.** Task 3's Step 8 shipped
`tip=$(git … rev-parse --verify "refs/heads/$branch") || tip=""`, `ahead=0` and
`dirty=$(… | grep -c . || true)`, and the ladder read `ahead == 0` as
`no-commits`. Measured on the shipped code: a `git branch -m ws/renamed` inside
the worktree — the state deviation 7 measured for `ws-archive` and calls
**ordinary** — turned a workspace holding `prphase=merged, prnumber=42` into
`{phase:"no-commits", ahead:0, tip:""}` and **removed `prnumber`**. A local
rename erased GitHub's answer: Task 14's auto-archive fires on
`prPhase === 'merged'` and could then never fire for that workspace, and
`cmd_ws_archive` had no number left to file as `archivedreason merged:#42`.

Three changes, one rule — *a number is a measurement, and null is what we say
when we did not measure*:

- **`--quiet` on the tip read, with git's two exit codes kept apart.** rc 1 =
  the ref does not resolve → `tip: null`. rc 128 = the repository cannot be read
  → the per-session failure object (`{"id":…,"phase":"unknown","reason":"error"}`),
  persisting nothing. Without `--quiet` git answers 128 for both and the two
  collapse — the exact distinction `_ws_archive_manifest` was written to
  preserve, a hundred lines up in the same file.
- **`ahead` is null whenever the tip is**, and `None == 0` is False in python,
  so the ladder falls through to `none` — "no PR bound here", which was
  observed — instead of `no-commits`, which asserts the branch is level with
  base. `phaseFor` mirrors it with `line.ahead === 0` over an
  `ahead: number | null`, and coerces only for `PrState.ahead`, which the cap
  renders.
- **Proof 0 skips the ancestry rung, rather than failing it, when `tip` is
  null.** `is_ours` answering False there is what demoted the bound MERGED row:
  a local fact overriding GitHub's. What remains is `cat-file -e` (the commit is
  in this repository) plus the three conjuncts that do not need a tip — not a
  fork, our base, our branch name. The recycled slug, which is the case the
  ancestry rung exists for, cannot be in this state: `ws-add` creates the
  branch, so a recycled name always resolves and always gets the full proof. The
  wire says which rung answered — `tip` is null beside `ours`.

`dirty`'s null is deviation 11. Consumers swept in the same round: `CcdPrLine`
(`tip`/`ahead`/`dirty` nullable), `phaseFor`, `prView`'s `facts`, `PrView` in
`shared/api.ts`, and `PrSheet`'s facts line and dirty advisory. Task 12's
agreement matrix gains the two rows this opens — a bound merge under a renamed
branch, and an unreadable gh body as a whole-repo failure — which is where
`phaseFor` had nothing to agree about before.

**11. `pr-state`'s `dirty` read is ENTITLED before it runs, and answers `null`
instead of refusing when it cannot be.** Step 8 shipped
`dirty=$(git -C "$workdir" status --porcelain 2>/dev/null | grep -c . || true)`.
Two defects in one line, both already legislated against in this execution.
The pipe discards git's status (there is no `PIPESTATUS` read), so a deleted
worktree reports `"dirty": 0` — a positive claim that nothing is uncommitted
about a directory that is not there. That is deviation 6's `_ws_ignored_digest`
defect verbatim (*"it hashed a silent empty stream … a failure on either side
manufactured the match"*), committed a hundred lines from Task 2's correct
two-statement version of the identical read. And Global Constraints require a
`-C "$workdir"` **tree** read to run only after `_ws_wt_branch` and
`_ws_common_dir` have both said `$main`; there was no such check, so a stranger
repository `git init`ed at a hand-deleted workdir had its dirt counted and filed
under this workspace.

The read now runs only behind that pair, in two statements with git's status
read on its own line. What it does **not** do is refuse: `pr-state` is
read-only, it runs for every workspace of a project from one `gh` call, and the
PR state is still perfectly knowable when the worktree is not — so an
unentitled or unreadable tree yields `dirty: null` plus one line on stderr, and
every other field is answered as normal. (`ws-archive` refuses on the same
facts because it writes a record that authorises deletions; the asymmetry is
the same one Task 2's Context draws.) `null` is not `0`: the composer's
"N files are not committed" advisory is silence when the count is unknown, and
silence there reads as "clean", so `PrSheet` says the unknown case out loud.

**12. `pr-open` asks GitHub through `_gh_pr_list`, which gains a head filter —
and both of its reads FAIL CLOSED.** Step 3 shipped the idempotence probe as
`existing=$(timeout "$PR_GH_TIMEOUT" gh pr list … 2>/dev/null)`, testing only
`-n` and `!= "[]"`. That captures stdout alone, and rc 124, an expired token, a
rate limit and an offline box all produce EMPTY stdout — indistinguishable from
"no PR". Measured with `gh` exiting 124 on the probe: rc 0, the branch on the
origin, one `pr create` issued. **A bounded write may not proceed on an unproven
"no PR exists"**, and the concrete loss is a duplicate PR whenever the existing
one is cross-repository, because our own create then succeeds.

`_gh_pr_list` (Task 3) already captured rc and classified stderr into
`timeout`/`unauthenticated`/`rate-limit`/`offline`, for this exact call. The verb
open-coded `gh pr list` twice instead. Both calls go through it now, so the
change to Task 3's contract is one optional second parameter — a **named** head
filter, with the flag built inside the function, never a forwarded `"$@"` (pflag
is last-wins on the one gh call two verbs share). `pr-state` passes none and its
argv is byte-identical to before.

Two consequences the plan owes out loud. `rc != 0` on the probe is now a
refusal naming the classified reason — "gh failed" would send the reader to
check `gh auth` for a box that is merely offline. And rc 0 is not the same as an
answer: `gh` writes diagnostics to STDOUT and exits 0, so `_gh_rows_ok` refuses
anything that is not a JSON list — including `{"message":"Not Found"}`, which is
what the API says about a repo the token cannot see and is perfectly good JSON.
That is `rows_in`'s rule (deviation 9's neighbour, `ccd:445-450`) applied to the
caller that never reaches python. The `-n` half of the old condition is gone
with it: a list is non-empty by construction, so it can no longer be a half
nothing tests. Same reader means the same 100-PR window and the same
`PR_JSON_FIELDS` on both paths, which is the second half of deviation 13.

**13. `pr-open`'s stdout is the PR and nothing else, and the refusal after a
partial write names what it left.** Three defects, one subject — what the verb
SAYS about a write that half-happened:

- `git push --set-upstream` prints *"branch 'x' set up to track 'origin/x'."* on
  **stdout**, so the created path's answer was that sentence followed by the
  rows: not JSON, and never asserted. The push's stdout is dropped; its ref
  summary and every failure are on stderr, which is what the route surfaces.
- The two `--json` lists (`number,url,state` and `number,url,state,isDraft`)
  made two success shapes out of one contract, so a caller could tell which path
  it had taken from a field that is supposed to describe the PR. One reader,
  one shape (deviation 12). A failed read-back says *the PR was opened* — it
  was, and that is the difference between "retry" and "look before you retry".
- `die "gh pr create failed"` said nothing about the branch it had just pushed
  and upstreamed. Reproduced: after a failed create, `refs/heads/ws/quiet-basin`
  is on the origin with `@{upstream}` set. The push is deliberately NOT rolled
  back — that ref is the workspace's own work, lossless, and what a retry needs
  to find there; an automatic `push --delete` would be a destructive rollback of
  a state nobody lost anything to — so the message names it instead, the way the
  push's own refusal says "nothing was opened" about a state where truly nothing
  was.

**14. Task 5's fixtures commit `.gitignore` INTO the merged work, and
`squashMovedBase` takes the ignore lines as a parameter.** The plan's own
fixtures committed `.gitignore` to the branch *after* the squash landed. That is
a commit genuinely not in the merge, so the ladder refuses `tree-differs` before
any question about ignored content is reached: `LISTS non-sensitive ignored
content` failed outright, and `changes the token when ANY fingerprinted fact
moves` **passed vacuously**, comparing a 64-hex token against the `undefined` a
refusal hands out. The lines now go into the branch's commits and into main's
squash of them, so both sides carry them and the patch-ids still match.

**15. `cmd_ws_audit` hands out no token for a worktree that is GONE, and says
`reap-interrupted` while doing so.** With a `reaping` breadcrumb,
`_ws_reap_eval` skips the whole of Phase B by design — that is the RESUME of a
killed reap, and refusing it would strand a workspace half-deleted forever — so
it reaches `reapable` with `REAP_DIRTY=0`, `REAP_IGNDIGEST=""` and
`REAP_SENSITIVE=()` straight out of `_ws_reap_reset`. Those are reset defaults,
not measurements: `dirty-tree` and `sensitive-ignored`, the two guards §7 forbids
overriding, were never evaluated, and a fingerprint over them is deviation 6's
digest forgery with more fields. `_ws_reap_eval` is deliberately unchanged (Task
6's resume depends on its `reapable`); the VERB withholds the token. And the
verdict changes with it — a tokenless `reapable` renders a dead button, because
`wsaudit.ts` gives `reapable` an empty sentence and `ReapSheet` puts the primary
Remove button on `verdict === 'reapable'` while its `confirm()` early-returns on
a missing token. Two states, two verdicts.

**16. Both Phase B reads check stderr, not only the exit code.** A PARTIALLY
unreadable tree makes git warn and exit 0: measured on git 2.43, `chmod 000` on
a subdirectory gives rc 0, no line for anything inside it, and `warning: could
not open directory 'sub/'` on stderr — which `2>/dev/null` threw away. The tree
then read pristine, `dirty-tree` passed, and `sensitive-ignored` could not fire
over files nobody enumerated. Any diagnostic is now a read that did not
complete, and the test is for the DIAGNOSTIC and not its wording, because git
translates warnings and ccd pins no locale. `_ws_ignored_digest` (Task 2) was
**not** widened; the forgery is closed on the audit/reap side.

**17. Three reads that answered a failure with a default now refuse, and the
`ignored` set is read `-z`.** Four separate holes, one class, all measured end
to end on the shipped verb:

- **The ignored set was read C-QUOTED.** `git status --porcelain
  --ignored=matching` quotes any path holding a space, a non-ASCII byte, a
  quote, a backslash or a control character — `!! .env` bare beside
  `!! "deploy key.pem"` and `!! "s\303\251crets/"` — so every suffix pattern in
  `_ws_sensitive_match` died on the trailing `"` and every prefix pattern on the
  leading one. A gitignored private key named `deploy key.pem` came back
  `verdict=reapable`, `sensitive:false`, `bytes:0`, **with a token**, against the
  guard §7 says has no override. `-z` is what fixes it (`core.quotePath=false`
  unquotes the non-ASCII byte and STILL quotes the space, measured), and it
  needs a temp file because command substitution drops NUL. Sizes come from
  `du -sb … | head -n1` rather than `_ws_gc_bytes`, which answers `-` for
  anything that is not a directory and made every ignored FILE 0 bytes.
- **`_ws_stash_count` reports every failure as 0.** Measured on git 2.43: with
  `.git/logs/refs/stash` unreadable OR deleted while `refs/stash` still
  resolves, `git stash list` returns rc 0, EMPTY stdout and EMPTY stderr — so
  neither a status check nor deviation 16's stderr rule can see it, and because
  the failure is deterministic ws-reap recomputes the same 0 and `--expect`
  matches. The helper is Task 2's and Task 4 consumes it, so it is NOT widened:
  the audit call site corroborates instead, against `refs/stash`. The invariant
  is ONE-WAY and the plan said "iff" until the second review round measured it:
  ≥1 entry **⇒** the ref resolves (measured across push/pop/drop/clear) is a law
  git keeps; the converse is not, and the converse is what the guard uses — see
  deviation 21. A ref that resolves beside an empty list refuses
  `stash-unreadable`. What it deliberately does not do is read the ref's
  existence as "this branch has stashes" — a stash on another branch is a
  legitimate reapable state, and refusing it would make every workspace in a
  repo whose main holds one stash permanently un-reapable.
- **`baseOid` defaulted to `""`.** Plan-verbatim, and the last fingerprint input
  that answered a failed read with a default: the verdict stayed `reapable` and
  a token was issued over a field nobody measured. It refuses `base-missing`.
- **The `_pr_py pick` TSV was split without re-anchoring.** `mergeCommit.oid`
  and `headRefOid` are checked against `OID` inside python, but `url` and
  `number` are GitHub-sourced and unanchored, and all four come back joined with
  tabs — so a `url` holding a TAB shifts the fields. Measured: `injected`
  became `REAP_MERGE` and reached three git revision operands. It failed closed,
  by luck rather than construction; §7 calls this boundary "not a formality", so
  the same regex is restated on this side of the split and refuses
  `pr-fields-malformed`.

**18. `REAP_IGNORED` records are `sensitive\tbytes\tpath`, not
`path\tbytes\tsensitive`.** Deviation 17's `-z` read is what forces it: git is no
longer escaping a TAB or a NEWLINE inside a path either, and a path-first record
read left to right shifts every field — measured, `a<TAB>b.log` made
`cmd_ws_audit` print `"bytes":b.log`, which is not JSON at all. The two
fixed-shape fields (one of `0|1`, one of `[0-9]+`, neither able to hold a tab)
go first and the free-form one last, the array is sorted `sort -z` and read
`read -d ''`, and the fields are peeled off the FRONT with `${…%%}`/`${…#}`
rather than by word-splitting, which would collapse a run of tabs. Task 6's
`_ws_tombstone` reads the same array and moves with it.

**19. `ws-audit` has three verdict shapes.** `reapable` **always** carries a
token; `reap-interrupted` is proven-but-tokenless (deviation 15); everything
else is a refusal with a detail. Stated as a contract because the PWA branches
on it: `reapable` is the only value that may render the Remove button, and the
button and the token are now impossible to separate.

**20. `_json_str` decodes RAW BYTES with `errors='replace'`, under a pinned
locale, and `cmd_ws_audit` probes it up front.** Deviation 17's `-z` read is
what forces this one too: it stopped git C-quoting paths into ASCII, so a
filesystem path — any byte string on Linux — now reaches the serializer whole.
`_json_str` read stdin through python's LOCALE codec, which under this box's
`LANG=en_US.UTF-8` is utf-8 STRICT: one 0xff byte raised `UnicodeDecodeError`,
stdout was empty, `$(…)` swallowed the status, and `cmd_ws_audit` printed
`"ignored":[{"path":,"bytes":600,…}]` — a document `JSON.parse` rejects, at
exit 0, over a workspace whose verdict was `sensitive-ignored` and whose
`sensitive` array had silently degraded to `[]`. Under `LC_ALL=C` the same
input was fine, so it was locale-dependent as well as wrong. The read is now
`sys.stdin.buffer` (no locale can reach it) decoded utf-8 `errors='replace'`,
with `LC_ALL=C.UTF-8` pinned rather than inherited. Lossy DELIBERATELY: every
decision over these bytes is already taken in bash on the RAW bytes
(`_ws_sensitive_match`'s globs, `du`'s size, `_ws_ignored_digest`'s hash)
before anything is serialised, so what is left is the human's copy and U+FFFD
is the honest rendering of a byte that is not text. `_json_str`'s non-zero now
means only "python3 could not be run", and `cmd_ws_audit` checks it ONCE up
front — the same probe `_ws_manifest` already had — because its nineteen
`_json_str` substitutions sit inside printf argument lists where a status is
swallowed by construction. A record that authorises deletions either parses or
is not printed.

**21. The stash guard's invariant is one-way, and its refusal carries the
remedy.** Deviation 17 adopted it as a biconditional — "`refs/stash` exists iff
at least one entry does" — and only half of that is a law git keeps. Measured
on git 2.43: `git reflog expire --all --expire=now --expire-unreachable=now`, a
documented maintenance command that does not mention refs/stash, empties the
stash reflog and LEAVES THE REF, so it resolves (rc 0) beside a `git stash list`
that returns rc 0 and zero entries — the exact shape the guard reads as "the
reflog was not read". (`git gc --prune=now` does not reach it, nor does gc with
`gc.reflogExpire=now`; git protects refs/stash from gc by default. Measured.)
The guard therefore has a false-positive state in which a repository that
honestly holds no stashes answers `stash-unreadable` PERMANENTLY, for every
workspace in it, with no override, and — running before the `exists` branch —
with the `reap-interrupted` resume path blocked too. It fails SAFE, so the guard
stays and the state is DISCLOSED rather than engineered away: the two are
indistinguishable from inside ccd and the only safe reading of "I cannot tell"
is to refuse. What changes is that a permanent, override-less refusal must name
its way out. `'git stash clear'` and `'git update-ref -d refs/stash'` are in the
refusal detail and in `wsaudit.ts`'s sentence — the sheet renders the SENTENCE,
not the detail, so a remedy that lived only in `detail` would never reach the
operator it is addressed to. Both remedies are measured against the
reflog-expire fixture in Task 5's test file.

**22. `_ws_sensitive_match` gains a `*.env` arm the spec's pattern set does not
list.** The spec (design §"sensitive", line 372) names `.env*` and nothing for
the other spelling, so `production.env`, `prod.env`, `staging.env` and
`My Project.env` were ordinary rubbish queued for deletion in the one guard §7
forbids overriding. Measured directly: `_ws_sensitive_match "My Project.env"`
returned 1. Four places claimed that case was closed by deviation 17's `-z`
read — this document twice, ccd's `_ws_collect_ignored` comment and Task 5's
C-quoting test — and all four were wrong in the same way: `-z` fixed the
QUOTING of `deploy key.pem` and `prod db.sqlite`, whose suffixes were already
listed, while `My Project.env` had no arm to match quoted or unquoted. All four
now say so. The arm is a SUFFIX, not a substring: `env.sample` and
`environment` are in the negative half of `matches EVERY pattern`, which is the
half that stops the list growing into something that refuses every workspace.
(`sécrets/` is NOT in the same class and stays non-sensitive: `secrets*` never
matched it quoted or unquoted, and the shipped test says so — the original
review's fixture for it was a mis-diagnosis, correctly disputed.)

**23. `cmd_ws_audit`'s `dirty` array is read `-z` too, and pairs renames.**
Deviation 17 unquoted the `ignored` list and left its sibling C-quoted in the
same document: measured, a dirty `déjà vu.txt` rendered
`"?? \"d\303\251j\303\240 vu.txt\""` beside an `ignored` array carrying raw
paths. No guard reads this array — `dirty-tree` refuses on `REAP_DIRTY`, a count
from `_ws_reap_eval`'s own read — so nothing here decides anything; it is the
manifest a human authorises a deletion from, which is the whole of why the
ignored list was a finding, and it now routes through deviation 20's serializer.
`-z` takes back what it gives here as well: porcelain v1 emits a rename or copy
as TWO NUL-terminated records (`XY <to>NUL<from>`) where the non-`-z` form
printed one `R  <from> -> <to>` line, so the second is consumed and rejoined —
unpaired it would join the list as an entry with no status letters, a bare
filename in the list a human is asked to read. Both letters are reachable and
both have fixtures: an INDEX rename for `R` (a worktree-only rename is not
detected at all — measured, ` D` plus `??`), and `status.renames=copies` with a
MODIFIED source for `C` (an unmodified source reports a plain `A`, because git's
copy detection only considers sources that changed in the same diff and status
has no `--find-copies-harder`). The read uses process substitution rather than a
temp file — that is a pipe, so NULs survive it; it is `$(…)` that drops them and
`_ws_collect_ignored` that therefore needs a file.

**24. `_ws_tombstone` writes the attic REF NAMES, not their count, and its
signature is `id clipsjson`.** The plan's Step 3 wrote `"attic":$attic` (a
number) while the plan's own Step 1 test asserted `Array.isArray(t.attic)` —
two statements of one decision that contradicted each other. Spec §5.5(b)
settles it: the tombstone contains "…the attic ref names, and the reflog dump",
and the COUNT is §5.5(j)'s, on the verb's stdout, where it stays. They are
different facts and both are needed: `ccd ws-attic --drop <id>` releases the
refs, and after that this document is the only record of which commits were
pinned — by then the branch, the reflog and the registry are all gone. The list
is read back from `for-each-ref` inside the helper so it has ONE producer and
cannot disagree with itself, which left the `atticrefs` parameter with no
reader, so it was dropped. Both call sites in this document move with it.

**25. `cmd_ws_reap` probes `_json_str` once up front and dies.** ccd:145-146
states the file's own rule — "both callers that build a whole record
(`_ws_manifest`, `cmd_ws_audit`) probe once up front" — and this is the third.
The record it builds is the TOMBSTONE, the one document that outlives the
workspace, and every `_json_str` in it sits inside a printf ARGUMENT LIST where
a failure is a swallowed status and an empty argument (`"path":,`). The resume
path is the one route into the destructive tail that never calls `_pr_py`, so
python3 being missing does not already refuse it: without the probe it would
delete and then report the deletion in a document that does not parse. Placed
after the argv asserts, before the lock (so a refusal leaves no lock file) and
before `_ws_reap_eval` (so it costs no gh call and no fetch).

**26. The `branch -D` ban is per LINE, not a substring scan of the file.** The
plan's Step 1 test banned the substring over the comment-stripped file, and
`cmd_ws_rm` PRINTS that command for an operator to run themselves (ccd:835) —
a line this plan's own resume test cites approvingly, and one Task 8 keeps
deliberately. As written the test could not pass. The single surviving
occurrence is now named and asserted, so a SECOND occurrence anywhere fails:
stricter than the ban it replaces, and true.

**27. The reap lock is a `flock`, not a `mkdir` plus an EXIT trap.** A trap does
not run on SIGKILL — an OOM kill (this box's own speciality), a `systemctl` hard
stop, a power loss, a reboot — so the lock directory survived its own process,
every later `ws-reap` for that session answered `in-progress`, and the RESUME
PATH, i.e. the entire recovery mechanism, sat one refusal behind a lock no verb
in ccd could clear. Measured, one fixture, only the signal changed: SIGTERM left
it free and the next run resumed; SIGKILL left it HELD for ever. `flock -n` on a
dedicated descriptor is released by the KERNEL when the last copy of that
description closes, so nothing has to run for it to come back (verified here on
util-linux 2.39.3, both directions). The description is inherited by children —
measured — which is the right semantics rather than a leak: the orphaned
`git worktree remove` grandchild the old comment worried about is exactly the
case in which a second reap must not start. The lock file is never unlinked,
because unlink-while-held is how two processes hold two inodes and each believes
it has the lock; the cost is a 0-byte hidden file per session, stated at the
site. The body moved into `_ws_reap_locked` so every return path closes the
descriptor: `flock` treats two `open()`s of one path in one process as
strangers, and ccd is sourced.

**28. The resume's tip re-validation is applied PER PHASE.** §5.6 says
"re-validate `refs/heads/$branch == $tip` from the tombstone, THEN continue from
the recorded phase", and applied unconditionally that is a contradiction for
`reaping=clips`: (g) has already CAS-deleted the branch by then, so the live ref
is empty BY CONSTRUCTION and the gate reads "moved" for the one phase in which
gone is correct — permanently. Measured: the clips directory leaked, the
registry row survived with no worktree and no branch, `ccd ls` and the PWA kept
showing it, and the detail said "nothing was deleted after the worktree" while
everything up to and including the branch had been. The tip's PRESENCE is still
required on every phase (it is the CAS old-value); only the comparison is per
phase, `clips` is the only phase that skips it, and the default arm re-validates
so a breadcrumb ccd never wrote gets the stricter reading. The same fixture pins
(g)'s `show-ref` gate in the SKIP direction, which nothing else in the file
could reach.

**29. Sensitivity is sampled INSIDE a collapsed ignored directory, with `find`.**
`--ignored=matching` collapses a wholly ignored directory to one entry, so
`build/.env` holding a live key was handed to `_ws_sensitive_match` as `build/`
and nothing ever looked inside: measured, verdict `reapable`, a token issued,
`sensitive: []`, and the key gone under a sheet reading "1 entry, 39 B —
build/". Moving one secret one directory deeper defeated the only guard §7
refuses to give an override. The enumeration is `find`, not
`git ls-files --others --ignored`: measured on git 2.43, git collapses a nested
repository exactly as `--ignored=matching` collapses a directory and never names
`build/nested/.env`, i.e. it reproduces this blindness one level deeper over
content `rm -rf` destroys all the same. All types, not `-type f`, because the
top-level matcher matches directory names too. Bounded by a whole-workspace 30 s
deadline rather than a per-entry timeout, so 226 ignored entries cannot cost 226
timeouts; measured against the tree `--ignored=matching` was chosen for
(custom-tools, 226 collapsed entries, 355,392 entries beneath them) the whole
scan costs 3.4 s. Expiry and any `find` diagnostic are reads that did not
complete, so they refuse `tree-unreadable` with the remedy in the message. The
glob list becomes ONE list with two consumers (`_ws_sensitive_match` and a
derived `find` predicate), because two hand-maintained copies of a §7 guard is
the drift this design cannot afford.

**30. The ignored digest is over the RECORDS, not over the paths.** It hashed
`status --ignored=matching`'s lines, i.e. the set of paths, so measured: growing
an ignored `build/out.o` from 9 bytes to 400,000 left the token IDENTICAL and
the reap deleted 400,215 bytes where the sheet said 9; adding a file inside an
already-listed ignored directory did the same; so did dropping a whole nested
git repository into one (27,141 bytes, reaped silently). The records already
carry `sensitive\tbytes\tpath`, so hashing them makes both the size and
deviation 29's sensitivity move the token. `_ws_ignored_digest` survives for the
ARCHIVE manifest, which records what it cannot describe rather than refusing.
One measured consequence: the collector's `(( rc == 0 ))` guard was a disclosed
mutation survivor only because the digest's second `git status` answered for it;
with that read gone it is killed by two existing tests, and both stale
disclosures are corrected.

**31. `cmd_ws_audit` publishes a `clips` manifest and the fingerprint has a
thirteenth fact.** The reap `rm -rf`s `~/.cc-clips/<id>` — full-resolution
pastes, the one thing in the workspace that exists nowhere else — and the
fingerprint could not see it: measured, two clips pasted between the sheet
rendering and the tap left the token identical and were deleted. That is a
change to WHAT GETS DELETED that no human consented to in any form, which is the
one thing D2 exists to refuse. The manifest comes from `_ws_clip_manifest`, the
same producer the tombstone records at (a), so the record of what was destroyed
and the consent to destroy it cannot name different files; `WsAudit`, the
`ReapSheet` row and the Task 13/17 fixtures move with it.

**32. The attic's 200-cap is applied to the REFLOG, then the tip is appended.**
It was applied to `{ reflog; tip } | sort -u`, i.e. to the union, so the tip was
just another line in hex-sort order. Measured on a workspace with 231 commits:
237 distinct reflog shas, the tip at rank 201, `tip pinned in attic? 0` — 200
refs written and not one of them the branch's own commit, which is the ONE
commit a squash merge leaves outside main and therefore the one the attic exists
for. Spec §5.5(a) reads "deduped, capped at 200, PLUS `tip`"; now so does the
code, with a second `sort -u` that dedupes rather than caps so a tip already
inside the 200 is not pinned twice. Two shipped disclosure sentences claimed
this could not happen; both corrected.

**33. What the resume path does NOT do is written down.** Three statements it
was making silently: `--expect` is never compared there (kept exempt — see the
Task 6 Context, which now says so where the token is introduced — because there
is nothing to compare against once Phase B has no tree and Phase C would need a
gh read an outage could withhold for ever); (d) `_ws_unsupervise` and (e)
`tmux kill-session` are never re-run (safe only because `not-archived` means
`cmd_ws_archive` already did both, which is now stated rather than assumed); and
its dirty read discards stderr no longer — a partially unreadable tree exits 0
with an empty stdout and a `warning:` on stderr, so the count is 0 and
`dirty-tree` passes. That last one is disclosed as a mutation survivor and
MEASURED as one: with stderr discarded again the whole suite is green, because
`_ws_collect_ignored` refuses first. It is defence in depth against exactly that
ordering being relied on.

**34. Three tests were added to Task 7's `ccd-ws-gc.test.ts` beyond its Step 1,
closing a gap the brief's own tests leave open.** The six given tests never
exercise `_ws_gc_row`'s `reaping` ladder rung or `_ws_gc_prune_row`'s
`reaping)` arm through a worktree that is still on disk — both "mid-reap"
fixtures there call `fs.rmSync` on the worktree first, which routes the row
through `dead-reg`/`stale-meta` instead, so a mutant that broke either
construct left the file's specified 41-test suite green. A workspace can be
mid-reap with its worktree fully present — that is exactly the window between
(c) and (f) in `_ws_reap_tail` — so three tests were added: a `reaping`-alone
ladder classification, a combined archived+reaping ladder classification
(which also pins that `reaping` is checked before `archived` — a real mid-reap
workspace has both markers set, since `_ws_reap_eval` refuses `not-archived`
otherwise, and the more actionable state must win), and `--prune`'s decline
message for a live mid-reap workspace.

**35. The Task 6 gate's required hardening: `_ws_reap_tail` fails closed on a
breadcrumb phase ccd never wrote.** The worktree-removal step was gated by
`[[ "$resumed" == "" || "$resumed" == worktree ]]` — LOOSE, because any value
that is neither `""` nor `worktree` falls to the same ELSE as a legitimate
`branch` or `clips` resume, so `git worktree remove` is silently skipped and
the run falls through to (g)'s branch delete, (h)'s clips delete and (i)'s
registry delete anyway, reporting `{"reaped":...}`. Measured: a breadcrumb of
`reaping=sometime-else` with the worktree still on disk finished with the
worktree still on disk (orphaned, still registered with git), the branch gone,
and the registry gone, on a run that claimed success. A `case "$resumed" in
""|worktree|branch|clips) : ;; *) <refuse> ;; esac` now runs before any of
those four steps, refusing `reaping-phase-unknown` (a new refusal token —
Task 13's `SENTENCES` table carries it, marked with this deviation number) and
deleting nothing. Two tests were added to
`ccd-ws-reap.test.ts`'s `describe('partial failure and resume', ...)`: the
guard itself, and a `branch`-breadcrumb resume — nothing in that file had
previously resumed a run FROM a `branch` breadcrumb (every fixture either
resumed from `worktree` or reached `branch` without a second reap call), so
without it the allow-list's `branch` arm was untested and a mutant dropping it
from the pattern left the suite green.

**36. `fleet.css`'s `.sess-sheet-remove` rule, and the comment above it, are
deleted too — a file Task 8's own Files list never names.** The mutation
sweep's revert-the-deletion check (put the rule back, run the full pwa suite)
SURVIVED: vitest's default `css: false` means jsdom never sees an imported
stylesheet's rules, so a `.className { color }` revert is invisible to every
test in the package. The one existing precedent for testing CSS here
(`primitives.test.tsx`'s `toHaveStyle` checks) asserts an inline `style`
attribute set by React, not a class selector's rule from an imported file —
there is no idiomatic way to pin this with a test. The rule's own comment had
already gone false (it justified a muted, non-red color by pointing at
`ws-rm`'s own stderr warning, which no PWA tap can see), so it is deleted
alongside the button that was its only consumer, and the survivor is
disclosed here rather than killed by a new assertion: introducing
computed-style testing to this package for one dead rule would be a larger
footprint than the thing it pins.

**37. A new test in `pwa/test/api.test.ts` — a file Task 8's own Files list
never names — pins that `api.workspaceRemove` no longer exists.** The
mutation sweep's revert-the-deletion check on `api.ts` found a real gap:
restoring both `del` and `workspaceRemove` together, without touching
`SessionActionsSheet.tsx`'s button at all, compiles clean under
`noUnusedLocals` (each now references the other) and leaves every test in the
pwa suite green, because nothing else in the client ever called
`workspaceRemove`. `expect('workspaceRemove' in api).toBe(false)` closes that
gap on the client's own shape, independent of any component happening to
render a button that calls it.

**38. `server/test/workspaces-route.test.ts`'s file-header comment is
rewritten; Step 1 specified only the test body.** The header said POST and
DELETE "just shell out to `ccd ws-add` / `ccd ws-rm`" — true of DELETE before
this task, false after: the route is gone and its test now pins a 404
instead. Left as written it would be exactly the kind of false comment Task 8
exists to remove from `SessionActionsSheet.tsx`. The rewrite states what POST
still does, what DELETE used to do, and that Task 17 lands its replacement.

**39. The agent package gains PATH containment — `test/contain-path.setup.ts`,
wired via `vitest.config.ts`'s `setupFiles` and pinned by
`test/contain-path.test.ts` — three files Task 9's own Files list never
names.** This is not tidying; it is the fix for a defect Task 9's own mutation
sweep discovered by triggering it. `exec.test.ts` asserts that
`{cmd:'tmux', args:['kill-server']}` comes back `forbidden`, and the agent
fixture isolates HOME but **not PATH** — so that argv resolves to the real
`tmux`, and the test is harmless only for as long as the whitelist it is
testing works. Under the widening mutant `tmux: [[]]` (an empty prefix matches
every argv, mutant M13/M14) the whitelist allowed it, the agent executed it,
and the box's tmux server died — taking all eleven ccrc sessions with it,
including the one driving the sweep. It happened three times before the cause
was understood: twice as an unexplained session restart, once as exit 137.
A negative test whose safety depends on the code under test is a loaded gun
pointed at the fleet, so the containment is structural rather than per-file:
one setup file puts a `tmux` that refuses everything earliest on PATH for every
agent test process, present and future, and cannot be lost by adding a test
file that forgets to ask. The pin runs the exact argv that killed the box and
asserts the stub answered, so the containment is proven by exercising it rather
than by asserting a config line. Agent suite 122 → 125.

The pin's FIRST version reproduced the very defect it guards, and it is worth
recording because the mistake is so easy to make twice: it called
`spawnSync('tmux', ['kill-server'])` and relied on the setup file to have made
that safe. Deleting the `setupFiles` line to watch the pin go red — the obvious
way to verify any pin, and precisely what a reviewer was asked to do — resolved
the real `tmux` and killed the fleet a **fourth** time. The pin now resolves
`tmux` once, asserts the resolution lies inside the contained directory, and
only then executes it **by absolute path, never by name**; with containment
removed it fails on that assertion and executes nothing. Verified both
directions: green when wired, three red assertions and an unchanged fleet when
the `setupFiles` line is deleted. The general rule this leaves behind: a test
that runs a destructive argv must prove the binary is a stub BEFORE running it,
and must never re-resolve that binary through PATH at call time.

**40. `isExecAllowed`'s `p.length <= args.length` conjunct carries a disclosed
mutation survivor.** Removing it leaves the whole suite green and always will:
when `args` is shorter than the prefix, `args[i]` reads `undefined` for the
overhanging indices, every `tok` is a string literal from `EXEC_WHITELIST`, and
`undefined === tok` is false — so `every` already answers false. The clauses
cannot disagree, because the line above rejects any non-string `args` element,
so no `undefined` can arrive as a value and make a short read compare equal.
It is a fast path, not a guard, and it is kept rather than deleted because it
states the prefix rule in the same breath as it checks it — and because
deleting it would make the widening mutants that removed the prefix ENTIRELY
read as ordinary edits rather than as the fleet-killing change they are. The
sweep's other 20 mutants — 14 widening, 4 narrowing, 1 crash — were all KILLED.

**41–45 were found by executing Task 10** (`ready.ccdVerbs` cross-box
capability and per-verb timeouts). 41 is a Files-list gap the brief's own
Step 1 instructions required closing anyway; 42 lists the mutation-sweep test
additions; 43–44 are the four disclosed survivors and one structural
re-arrangement the sweep found, re-synced into the Step 3/4/5 blocks above;
45 reconciles the measured counts, including a concurrent, unrelated commit

**46. The containment stub list covers `gh` as well as `tmux`

real credentialed binary. It was right, and the consequence is retrospective.
`M01_ADD_GH` adds a `gh: [['pr']]` grant; `exec.test.ts` sends
`gh pr create --repo o/r --head x --base main --title t --body b` expecting
`forbidden`; under that mutant the prefix matches, so the original sweep had
the agent execute the REAL `gh` — carrying this box's `repo`-WRITE-scoped
token, the one the whole design refuses to put behind a whitelist — against
GitHub. It failed only because `o/r` does not exist. The mutant was killed for
the right reason by the wrong mechanism: a live authenticated write attempt.
The stub list's admission rule is therefore not "what do the tests call today"
but **"what could a wrong whitelist make them call tomorrow"**, which is the
only circumstance containment exists for. `ccd` needs no stub — it resolves to
`$HOME/.local/bin/ccd` inside the fixture home, already isolated. Pinned by a
fourth test in `contain-path.test.ts` carrying the same
prove-the-binary-is-a-stub-before-running-it gate as the `tmux` one.

backgrounded in future tasks either.

**56. Task 11's layer 2b inverted from a blacklist to a whitelist (Task 11
review round 1, Finding 1).** The shipped rule banned inline argv array
literals at a `runCcd(...)`/`ccd(...)` call site — a trivial refactor defeats
it twice over: extracting `const argv = ['ensure', id]` before the call, or
moving the construction into a same-file helper function, both left
`whitelist-subset.test.ts` green at 35/35 while reproducing the exact
ws-add/ws-rm failure class the mechanism exists to prevent (reproduced against
the original rule before fixing it). Replaced with three checks over every
`.ts` file in `src/` except `ccdargv.ts`/`exec.ts`: every `runCcd(` call's
argv argument must BE a direct `CCD_ARGV.<name>(...)` call expression (or a
two-way ternary of exactly two such calls — the `enable`/`start` picker's
shape); `ccd(` may be called at most once outside those two files, and only
as `runCcd`'s own forwarding call (its argv argument must be the bare
parameter name `runCcd`'s own definition declares, extracted programmatically
so a rename can't silently stop being checked); and zero direct
`deps.run(`/`this.run(` bypasses. Both reviewer bypasses re-reproduced against
the fix: both now red. A legitimate `CCD_ARGV.ensure(id)` call, and the whole
existing route-test corpus, still pass (76/4 on the targeted files; full
suite below). Disclosed rather than implied, in a comment at the rule:
deliberate obfuscation (comma-operator tricks, dynamic member access, a local
`CCD_ARGV` shadow) is out of scope, string/template literals aren't parsed,
and — found empirically during the deviation-60 mutation sweep below —
comments are NOT stripped before scanning for `ccd(`, so the literal
substring `ccd(` inside a comment anywhere in a scanned file's `src/` (outside
`ccdargv.ts`/`exec.ts`) is misread as a call site. No shipped comment
currently contains it, so it is not a live false positive, but the scan
cannot currently tell the difference.

**57. `verbSupported`'s null-vs-`[]` distinction, pinned (Task 11 review round
1, Finding 2).** Mutating `if (verbs === null)` to
`if (verbs === null || verbs.length === 0)` left the whole suite green —
nothing exercised `ccdVerbs: []` against `verbSupported` (only `null` and a
populated array). The distinction is load-bearing: `null` means "no evidence
yet" (a reconnect in flight — permit); `[]` means the fleet ACTIVELY reported
zero verbs — refuse. Conflating them would silently re-permit everything for
the duration of a state meant to grey the whole feature out. No production
code changed — `verbSupported`'s existing `if (verbs === null) return true;`
already handled `[]` correctly (falls through to `.includes`, `false` on an
empty array); only the test coverage was missing. Added a new test pinning
both directions (`wsReap`, which needs a specific grant, and `ensure`, which
would otherwise read as universally uncontroversial); verified red against
the described mutant, then restored.

**59. A pre-existing `test/` type error in `whitelist-subset.test.ts`, fixed

and out of this task's authority): this error is gone; the sibling error in

**62. Task 12's review found the 52-mutant sweep incomplete, not merely
imperfect: `checksFor`'s two classic-commit-status fallbacks were
exercised by nothing.** `stateOf`'s `?? c.state` and `nameOf`'s
`?? c.context` exist for GitHub's older Status API shape
(`{state, context}`), which real repos still report through, sometimes
alongside the newer Checks API shape (`{conclusion, status, name}`) during
an incremental migration — but every fixture anywhere in the codebase,
including every existing `checksFor` test, supplied only the Checks API
shape. The review reproduced the consequence directly: removing
`?? c.state` left the full narrow suite (124/124) green, meaning a
repository reporting through classic statuses would silently render a
failing or pending check as `pass` — a lie about merge-readiness in the
one place this feature exists to tell the truth. Two tests were added
(a classic-status fixture covering both a failing and a pending case, and
a mixed Checks-API-plus-classic-status rollup, since real repos migrate
incrementally and carry both shapes in one rollup); two new mutants
(M53: drop `?? c.state`; M54: drop `?? c.context`) were added to the
matrix and each proven red-then-green individually, sha256-verified clean
before and after. The code itself was correct as shipped — this was a
test-coverage gap, not a shipped bug — but it means Task 12's original
report overstated the sweep's completeness, which is corrected in the
Task 12 report alongside the fix.

**77. `RunResult` does not exist; `Deps.runCcd` returns `Promise<CcdResult>`,
and `lifecycle.ts` — not in the brief's Files list — gains the binder that
makes it (Task 13S).** The brief's `Deps` block writes
`runCcd: (argv: CcdArgv) => Promise<RunResult>`; there is no `RunResult` in
this codebase (`exec.ts` has `ExecResult`, `lifecycle.ts` has `CcdResult`, and
`CcdResult` is what every route already consumes as `res.ok`/`res.stdout`/
`res.stderr`). Shipped as `CcdResult`. Three further pieces the brief did not
name follow from it: `ccd()`'s own `args` parameter is branded too (so even
the composition root cannot call it with a raw array), a `CcdRunner` type
alias, and `ccdRunner(run, cfg)` — the factory that binds a `Runner` plus a
config into the single capability, which `index.ts` and `testDeps` both use.
Without a factory every construction site would have to spell the closure
itself, and "the composition root is the only place a `Runner` is in scope"
would be a convention rather than a fact. Relatedly, `guardRunner` stays at
the `Runner` level rather than moving to `CcdRunner` as the brief's Step 4
suggests: one guard then covers BOTH the ccd path and the `Tmux` path, which
is exactly what Task 11's `M30`/`M31` pin; wrapping at `CcdRunner` would have
needed a second, differently-shaped guard for `Tmux` and duplicated the
whitelist assertion.

**79. The brief's fourth type-level pin COMPILES by design and was replaced;
`@ts-expect-error` was rejected as unpinnable here (Task 13S).** Step 6 offers
`(deps as { run?: unknown }).run` as the "`run` is not on Deps" pin. That
assertion is legal TypeScript and produces no error: an OPTIONAL property is
satisfied by its absence, so `Deps` really is assignable to
`{ run?: unknown }`. Shipped instead as the plain member access `void deps.run;`,
which yields TS2339. The brief also offers `@ts-expect-error` as "acceptable
and cheapest": rejected, because `server/tsconfig.json` excludes `test/` and
vitest has no typecheck block (CONSTRAINTS.md's own standing warning), so an
`@ts-expect-error` in a server test is evaluated by NO gate — a pin that cannot
fail. The shipped form spawns `tsc --noEmit` over two fixture projects and
asserts the exact `TSxxxx` code set per fixture file, so a fixture that starts
failing for an unrelated reason (a typo, a moved import) is a test failure
rather than a pin quietly gone decorative.

**82. What the old layer 2b enforced and the new mechanism does NOT (Task
13S).** Disclosed rather than implied. (a) Layer 2b banned `this.run(`
anywhere in `src/` outside `exec.ts`. A NEW class that privately holds a
`Runner` handed to it by `index.ts` — as `Tmux` legitimately does — is not
visible to the type system, and nothing replaces that ban. Mitigation is
structural, not enforced: `Runner` values exist only in `exec.ts`
(`realRunner`), `remote/client.ts` (`fleet.runner`), and `index.ts`, which is
the composition root. (b) Layer 2b scanned ALL of `src/`, including files that
never see `Deps`; the new mechanism is scoped to what flows through `Deps` and
`ccd()`. (c) **CORRECTED (pre-merge fix round, finding 13S-F1) — this bullet
originally named only "a deliberate cast" as the residual class; that
understated it.** Three cast-free shapes launder an arbitrary argv past the
brand: `Object.assign` onto a minted argv
(`Object.assign(CCD_ARGV.ensure('x'), ['ws-rm','evil'])` types as
`CcdArgv & string[]`, and was RUNTIME-VERIFIED to mutate the real argv in
place); array covariance (`const w: (readonly string[])[] = slots; w[0] =
[...]`); and any `any`-typed value flowing in uncast (e.g.
`JSON.parse(...)`) — alongside the originally-named deliberate cast
(`['ws-rm','x'] as unknown as CcdArgv`, exactly as
`(deps.tmux as unknown as { run: Runner }).run` still reaches `Tmux`'s
private runner). The fix round closed the `Object.assign` shape —
`ccdargv.ts`'s mint site now freezes every array it returns, so that
assignment throws instead of silently succeeding — and left the other three
disclosed rather than claimed closed: array covariance and `any` are
inherent to TypeScript's structural and gradual typing and cannot be closed
by a stronger brand. What IS closed, and was not before,
is the class layer 2b kept losing to: ordinary code, honestly written, naming
a value in a way the scanner had not been taught. `guardRunner` remains the
runtime backstop on both paths regardless of how an argv was built.

GB')).toBeInTheDocument()` — this fails: `getByText` requires a DOM node

<p className="archive-total">{`${count} archived · `}<span className="archive-total-bytes">{humanBytes(bytes)}</span></p>

(`reap-sheet.test.tsx`), and FleetScreen briefly showing one session's

(`fleet-screen.test.tsx`) — because the ONE mounted `ReapSheet` instance
