Insert after `cmd_ws_audit`:

```bash
_ws_attic_pin() {   # main id workdir tip -> echoes how many refs were created
  # Every distinct sha in the worktree's HEAD reflog, deduped and capped, plus
  # the tip. ~50 bytes each, no new objects, and the commits become REFERENCED
  # rather than dangling — so gc.pruneExpire can never reach them.
  #
  # TWO MUTATION SURVIVORS, disclosed and each measured (the `head -200` that
  # used to be a third is now half of the pinned ORDER below):
  #   - `git cat-file -e "${sha}^{commit}" || continue` is removable with the
  #     suite green: `update-ref` refuses a value it cannot resolve, so a
  #     nonexistent object creates no ref and increments nothing either way.
  #     It stays for the `^{commit}` PEEL rather than for the existence test —
  #     `update-ref` will happily point a ref outside refs/heads at a blob or a
  #     tree, and the attic is a record of COMMITS. No reflog can produce one,
  #     which is why no fixture can pin it.
  #   - `[[ -d "$workdir" ]] &&` is removable for the same reason: this helper
  #     is called only from the tail's `[[ -z "$resumed" ]]` arm, where Phase A
  #     has already proved the directory is $main's worktree. With it gone the
  #     read errors into /dev/null and the tip still comes through. It stays so
  #     the helper is safe to call from anywhere, which is how the resume path
  #     would want to call it if it ever did.
  #
  # THE CAP IS ON THE REFLOG, AND THE TIP IS APPENDED AFTER IT. It used to be
  # applied to `{ reflog; tip } | sort -u`, i.e. to the UNION, which made the tip
  # just another line in hex-sort order — measured end to end on a workspace
  # with 231 commits: 237 distinct reflog shas, the tip at rank 201 of them,
  # `tip pinned in attic? 0`, 200 refs written and not one of them the branch's
  # own commit. That commit is the ONE a squash merge leaves outside main, so it
  # is precisely the commit the attic exists for; after `origin/<branch>` is
  # auto-deleted on merge and the next `fetch --prune` runs, it is dangling with
  # the two-week fuse §5.5(a) exists to remove. Spec §5.5(a) reads "deduped,
  # capped at 200, PLUS `tip`", and now so does this: `sort -u | head -200` over
  # the reflog, then the tip, then a second `sort -u` — which dedupes rather
  # than caps, so a tip already among the 200 is not pinned twice and does not
  # inflate the count the sheet prints. At most 201 refs.
  #
  # What IS pinned, by `pins the tip when the reflog cannot be read, and makes
  # no ref from a non-sha`: the shape check (without it `refs/heads/main` is a
  # string `update-ref` resolves, and the attic grows a ref made out of a NAME)
  # and the unconditional tip append; by `pins the tip even past the 200-ref
  # cap`: the ORDER of the cap and the append; and by `pins the amended-away
  # commit` the first `sort -u`, because `%H` prints one line per reflog ENTRY
  # and the count that reaches the sheet has to be the number of refs that
  # exist. The cap's own MAGNITUDE — 200 rather than 20 — remains unpinned:
  # bounding it costs a fixture with 200 resolvable commits in it, and the
  # fixture above pins where the cap is applied without paying for how big it is.
  local main="$1" id="$2" workdir="$3" tip="$4" sha n=0
  while read -r sha; do
    [[ "$sha" =~ ^[0-9a-f]{40}$ ]] || continue
    git -C "$main" cat-file -e "${sha}^{commit}" 2>/dev/null || continue
    git -C "$main" update-ref "refs/ccrc/attic/$id/$sha" "$sha" 2>/dev/null && n=$(( n + 1 ))
  done < <( { [[ -d "$workdir" ]] && git -C "$workdir" reflog show --all --format=%H 2>/dev/null | sort -u | head -200; \
              printf '%s\n' "$tip"; } | sort -u )
  echo "$n"
}

_ws_clip_manifest() {   # id -> JSON array of {name,bytes}, and nothing else
  # Pre-merge fix round, finding A — the EIGHTH instance of the
  # measurement-forgery class (deviation 10), and the one where two sides
  # AGREE on a value NEITHER measured: the wire manifest, the fingerprint
  # (`clipsDigest`, `_ws_reap_eval`) and the tombstone (`_ws_tombstone`) all
  # come from this ONE producer, so all three inherited its blind spot.
  #
  # The old enumeration was `for f in "$dir"/*` filtered by `[[ -f "$f" ]]` —
  # depth-1, non-dot, REGULAR FILES ONLY. Step (h) (`_ws_reap_tail`, ccd:3203)
  # is `rm -rf "$cdir"` on the WHOLE DIRECTORY. Measured: with `clip-a.png`
  # (10 B) present, an audit issued a token; adding `.hidden-secret.png`
  # (4 KB) and `archive/{prod.env,big.bin}` (1 MB) left the manifest AND the
  # token byte-identical; the STALE token from before those files existed
  # still validated a reap; the whole directory — dotfile, subdirectory and
  # all — was destroyed; the tombstone still names only `clip-a.png`. Fixed
  # by enumerating with `find -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1`, which unlike a bare
  # glob does not skip dotfiles, and by sizing a DIRECTORY entry with `du -sb`
  # (recursive) rather than `stat`, whose size is the inode's, not its
  # contents' — so the enumeration now matches exactly what (h) destroys.
  # `sort -z` keeps the manifest deterministic across two calls over an
  # unchanged directory, the property the digest and the CAS both depend on
  # — `find`'s own enumeration order is a filesystem implementation detail,
  # not a promise, even though it happens to be stable on THIS box for an
  # unmodified small directory (measured: the token is identical across two
  # back-to-back audits with or without this line, which is why it is a
  # disclosed survivor rather than a pinned one — the fixture that would
  # distinguish them needs a filesystem, or a directory history, this suite
  # cannot arrange). Kept anyway, the same judgement the attic's 200-ref cap
  # gets for the identical reason (CONSTRAINTS.md): a property this design
  # depends on must not rest on an implementation detail merely because
  # today's filesystem happens to make it hold.
  #
  # TWO MORE MUTATION SURVIVORS, disclosed, both pre-existing this fix and
  # both still true of it. `[[ -d "$dir" ]] || { echo "[]"; … }` is removable with
  # the suite green because `find` on a nonexistent path prints nothing on
  # stdout and a diagnostic on stderr (discarded below), so the loop reads no
  # records either way — it stays as the early return that makes the empty
  # answer a DECISION rather than an accident of `find`'s own exit code, which
  # this function does not otherwise check. `|| echo 0` on a file's size fires
  # only if the entry disappears between the `find` and the `stat`, which no
  # fixture can arrange; it stays for the reason it always did — the
  # alternative is `"bytes":`, a document that does not parse, in the record
  # that outlives the workspace.
  local id="$1" dir="$HOME/.cc-clips/$id" f name b out="[" first=1
  [[ -d "$dir" ]] || { echo "[]"; return 0; }
  while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do
    name="$(basename "$f")"
    if [[ -d "$f" ]]; then
      # A directory's own size is the directory ENTRY's — `du -sb`, the same
      # recursive read `_ws_gc_bytes` uses, is what makes this figure the
      # bytes `rm -rf` actually reaches rather than one inode. Falling back
      # to `0` when `du` cannot fully read it is the SAME choice this
      # function's sibling fallback already makes for a file that vanishes
      # between the `find` and the `stat` (disclosed above): the byte count
      # in the display total can understate, but the entry's NAME still
      # lands in the manifest either way, which is what the digest and the
      # token — the actual consent boundary — are built from. Not the same
      # question `_ws_gc_bytes`'s own fix (finding F) answers: that fallback
      # protects a number a human reads on a confirm BUTTON before deciding;
      # this one protects a name a stale token's digest has to move on.
      b=$(du -sb "$f" 2>/dev/null | cut -f1); [[ "$b" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || b=0
      name="$name/"
    else
      b=$(stat -c %s "$f" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)
    fi
    (( first )) || out+=","; first=0
    out+="{\"name\":$(_json_str "$name"),\"bytes\":$b}"
  done < <(find "$dir" -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 -print0 2>/dev/null | sort -z)
  echo "$out]"
}

_reap_paths_json() {   # -> REAP_SENSITIVE as a JSON array of strings
  # Shared by BOTH refusal sites in cmd_ws_reap (the evaluated one and the
  # resume one), so the two cannot describe the same finding differently — and
  # both sites are now pinned, one per fixture, because a shared helper with one
  # caller under test is a shared helper by intention only.
  #
  # MUTATION SURVIVOR, disclosed: `[[ -n "$p" ]] || continue` is removable with
  # the suite green, exactly as its two siblings in `_ws_collect_ignored` and
  # `cmd_ws_audit` are. REAP_SENSITIVE is filled by the collector, which already
  # refuses an empty path, so no fixture can put one here. Kept as defence in
  # depth against a future producer, which is the same reason given there.
  local out="[" first=1 p
  for p in "${REAP_SENSITIVE[@]-}"; do
    [[ -n "$p" ]] || continue
    (( first )) || out+=","; first=0
    out+="$(_json_str "$p")"
  done
  printf '%s]\n' "$out"
}

_ws_tombstone() {   # id clipsjson -> writes .reaped/<id>.json, echoes its path
  local id="$1" clips="$2" dir="$REG/.reaped" f="$REG/.reaped/$1.json"
  mkdir -p "$dir"
  # `sensitive\tbytes\tpath`, NUL-terminated, read exactly as cmd_ws_audit reads
  # it (Task 5, deviation 18): the collector's `git status … -z` leaves a TAB or
  # a NEWLINE in a path intact, so the two fixed-shape fields come off the FRONT
  # and the path is everything after the second tab. A `read -r p b s` on a
  # path-first record shifts every field, and this record is what the TOMBSTONE
  # says was destroyed — the one document that outlives the workspace. The field
  # ORDER is pinned by `records in the tombstone the ignored manifest it
  # destroyed, field for field`, whose ignored entry is named `a<TAB>b.log`;
  # before that fixture existed every other one here had an EMPTY ignored set,
  # so this whole loop was unreached and the order was an argument rather than a
  # measurement.
  #
  # SEVEN MUTATION SURVIVORS in this function, disclosed together because six of
  # them are one reason — the tombstone is written on the EVALUATED path only,
  # after Phase A proved the registry complete and Phase C proved the PR, so the
  # states these lines are about cannot occur where they run:
  #   - `if (( ${#REAP_IGNORED[@]} ))` — on bash 4.4+ an empty array under
  #     `set -u` expands to nothing and the loop reads one empty record and
  #     skips it. The guard is what stops the empty case depending on that.
  #   - `[[ -n "$p" ]] || continue` and `[[ -n "$aref" ]] || continue` — neither
  #     producer can emit an empty record (gate finding N8's class, and the same
  #     answer: the next statement dereferences the value into a document a
  #     human reads filenames out of).
  #   - `[[ -d "$(_reg_get "$id" workdir)" ]] &&` on the reflog — the workdir
  #     exists whenever (b) runs; it stays so an empty `reflog` is a decision.
  #   - `| head -200` on the reflog — a cap, unpinnable for the reason
  #     `_ws_attic_pin`'s MAGNITUDE is (where the cap is APPLIED is pinned there
  #     now, by `pins the tip even past the 200-ref cap`; how big it is still
  #     costs a fixture with 200 resolvable commits in it, and this dump is not
  #     read by any guard at all).
  #   - the `REAP_PRNUM` numeric test — Phase C proved a bound merged PR before
  #     this line can run, so it is always numeric HERE. The sibling in
  #     `_ws_reap_tail`'s printf is genuinely reachable (the resume path prints
  #     an empty one) and is pinned there; this one is the same shape kept for
  #     the same reason, `"pr":` being invalid JSON.
  # The seventh is `|| transcript=""`, which cannot change anything at all: a
  # bare `VAR=$(cmd)` already assigns "" when cmd fails. It is written because
  # `cmd_ws_audit` (ccd:2161) writes it, and these two records name the same
  # transcript — they are kept identical so they cannot drift.
  local ign_json="[" first=1 rec rest p b s
  if (( ${#REAP_IGNORED[@]} )); then
    while IFS= read -r -d '' rec; do
      s="${rec%%$'\t'*}"; rest="${rec#*$'\t'}"
      b="${rest%%$'\t'*}"; p="${rest#*$'\t'}"
      [[ -n "$p" ]] || continue
      (( first )) || ign_json+=","; first=0
      ign_json+="{\"path\":$(_json_str "$p"),\"bytes\":$b,\"sensitive\":$( ((s)) && echo true || echo false)}"
    done < <(printf '%s\0' "${REAP_IGNORED[@]}")
  fi
  ign_json+="]"
  # THE ATTIC REF NAMES, not the count of them — spec §5.5(b) lists "the attic
  # ref names" among what this document contains, and (j) is where the count
  # goes, on the verb's stdout. They are different facts and both are needed:
  # `ccd ws-attic --drop <id>` releases the refs, and after that this document
  # is the only record of which commits were pinned — which is the whole point
  # of a tombstone, since by then the branch, the reflog and the registry are
  # all gone. Read back from git rather than passed in, so the list has ONE
  # producer and cannot disagree with itself; `_ws_attic_pin` has already
  # created them by the time (b) runs, and its own answer is "how many I
  # created", which is not the same question.
  local main="$PROJECTS_ROOT/$(_reg_get "$id" project)" attic_json="[" afirst=1 aref
  while IFS= read -r aref; do
    [[ -n "$aref" ]] || continue
    (( afirst )) || attic_json+=","; afirst=0
    attic_json+="$(_json_str "$aref")"
  done < <(git -C "$main" for-each-ref --format='%(refname)' "refs/ccrc/attic/$id/" 2>/dev/null)
  attic_json+="]"
  local reflog="" transcript
  [[ -d "$(_reg_get "$id" workdir)" ]] && reflog=$(git -C "$(_reg_get "$id" workdir)" reflog show --all --format='%H %gs' 2>/dev/null | head -200)
  transcript=$(_transcript_path "$id") || transcript=""
  {
    printf '{"id":%s,"project":%s,"workdir":%s,"branch":%s,"base":%s,"tip":%s,' \
      "$(_json_str "$id")" "$(_json_str "$(_reg_get "$id" project)")" \
      "$(_json_str "$(_reg_get "$id" workdir)")" "$(_json_str "$(_reg_get "$id" branch)")" \
      "$(_json_str "$(_reg_get "$id" base)")" "$(_json_str "$REAP_TIP")"
    printf '"uuid":%s,"wrapper":%s,"mergeCommit":%s,"proof":%s,"pr":%s,"prUrl":%s,' \
      "$(_json_str "$(_reg_get "$id" uuid)")" "$(_json_str "$(_reg_get "$id" wrapper)")" \
      "$(_json_str "$REAP_MERGE")" "$(_json_str "$REAP_PROOF")" \
      "$( [[ "$REAP_PRNUM" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] && echo "$REAP_PRNUM" || echo null)" "$(_json_str "$REAP_PRURL")"
    printf '"ignored":%s,"clips":%s,"transcript":%s,"attic":%s,"reflog":%s,"reapedAt":%s}\n' \
      "$ign_json" "$clips" "$(_json_str "$transcript")" "$attic_json" "$(_json_str "$reflog")" "$(date +%s)"
  } > "$f"
  echo "$f"
}
```

```bash
_ws_tombstone_reclip() {   # id clipsjson -> rewrites an EXISTING tombstone's
                            # `clips` field in place; non-zero if it could not.
  # Pre-merge fix round, finding E, same underlying gap as finding A: the
  # resume path re-proves Phase B and Phase D1 in full but never re-reads
  # `_ws_clip_manifest` — `tomb` on the resume branch is just the EXISTING
  # file's path (ccd:3149) — so a clip pasted between the original consent
  # and the resume is `rm -rf`'d at (h) and appears in NO record at all.
  # Measured: a 3 MB clip pasted after the tombstone was written was
  # destroyed on resume, and the tombstone still named only the first one.
  # The tokenless resume is disclosed and defensible (the tombstone IS the
  # consent record, ccd:2916-2933); the undisclosed half this closes is that
  # the record has to cover what THIS run destroys, not what the original
  # run saw.
  #
  # Only the `clips` field moves. `ignored`/`attic`/`reflog`/`pr`/`proof` etc.
  # keep whatever the ORIGINAL evaluated run measured — re-deriving them here
  # would need Phase C re-run (deliberately not, ccd:2929-2931) and Phase B's
  # full ignored-set walk (the resume only re-proves dirty/sensitive-ignored
  # as REFUSALS, ccd:3057-3068 — it never rebuilds `ignored[]` as a document).
  # `clips` is the one field this resume both re-measures AND is about to
  # destroy, so it is the one field this rewrites.
  #
  # Read-modify-write through python end to end, not a bash-side field
  # substitution: the existing document's every OTHER field has to survive
  # untouched, including ones this shell was never handed (`ignored`, `pr`,
  # `attic`, `reflog`). `separators=(",", ":")` matches `_json_str`'s own
  # compact style (no spaces) — without it a round-trip through python's
  # default `json.dump` changes every byte in the file even when `clips`
  # itself did not change, which would silently break
  # `_ws_reap_tail`'s own promise (ccd:3055-3061, the ORIGINAL wording this
  # finding narrows rather than removes) that an unrelated resume leaves the
  # journal alone.
  #
  # Failure is REFUSED, not swallowed — measured with a real permission
  # error (`chmod 444` on the tombstone file itself, which is what actually
  # blocks python's `open(…, "w")`; a directory-only chmod does not, since
  # overwriting an EXISTING file needs write on the FILE, not on the
  # directory that holds it). The caller turns a non-zero return here into
  # `tombstone-unwritable` before (h) runs — never destroy clips a document
  # could not be made to name truthfully.
  #
  # MUTATION SURVIVOR, disclosed: `[[ -s "$f" ]] || return 1` is removable
  # with the suite green. By the time either call site reaches this
  # function the tombstone is either the one `_ws_tombstone` just wrote at
  # (b) in THIS process, or the resume path's own `tombtip` read (ccd's
  # `_ws_reap_locked`) already proved a non-empty tombstone exists moments
  # earlier — no fixture can arrange this function running with the file
  # genuinely absent. Kept as the same "refuse rather than guess" instinct
  # every other guard in this file states for itself, not because a test
  # can currently force the branch.
  local id="$1" clips="$2" f="$REG/.reaped/$1.json"
  [[ -s "$f" ]] || return 1
  printf '%s' "$clips" | python3 -c '
import json, sys
path = sys.argv[1]
clips = json.loads(sys.stdin.read())
with open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    doc = json.load(fh)
doc["clips"] = clips
with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    json.dump(doc, fh, separators=(",", ":"))
' "$f" 2>/dev/null
}
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Add `cmd_ws_reap`**

Insert after `_ws_tombstone`:

```bash
cmd_ws_reap() {   # ccd ws-reap --expect <token> --session <id>
  # The ONLY destructive verb. Every guard is re-evaluated HERE, on the box, at
  # the instant of deletion — the audit's verdict is not trusted, it is
  # recomputed. A refusal prints on stdout and exits 0: it is an answer.
  [[ $# -eq 4 && $1 == --expect && $3 == --session ]] \
    || die "usage: ccd ws-reap --expect <token> --session <id>"
  local token=$2 id=$4
  [[ $token =~ ^[0-9a-f]{64}$ ]]    || die "bad token"
  [[ $id =~ ^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$ ]]    || die "bad session id"

  # `_json_str`'s status, checked ONCE and up front — the same probe, for the
  # same reason, as `cmd_ws_audit` (ccd:2153) and `_ws_manifest` (ccd:1109).
  # This is the THIRD caller that builds a whole record, and the record it
  # builds is the TOMBSTONE: the one document that outlives the workspace, and
  # the only thing left naming the transcript once step (i) has removed the
  # registry. Every `_json_str` here sits inside a printf ARGUMENT LIST, where a
  # failure is a swallowed status and an empty argument — `"path":,` — so
  # without this the resume path, which is the one route to the destructive tail
  # that never calls `_pr_py` and so is not already refused by python3 being
  # missing, would delete and then report it in a document that does not parse.
  # Before the lock, so a refusal leaves no lock behind for the next attempt to
  # trip over, and before `_ws_reap_eval`, so it costs no gh call and no fetch.
  _json_str probe >/dev/null 2>&1 \
    || die "python3 unavailable — cannot quote the reap record safely"

  # BEFORE either path, because ccd runs under `set -u` and `_ws_reap_tail`
  # reads REAP_PRNUM and REAP_PROOF unconditionally. On the resume path
  # `_ws_reap_eval` is never called, so without this they are UNBOUND, and the
  # final printf loses those two arguments: it emits {"pr":,"proof":} —
  # syntactically invalid JSON, which the caller reports as a parse error rather
  # than as the successful resume it actually was. (Reproduced in bash: two
  # `unbound variable` lines on stderr and a truncated object on stdout, exit 0.)
  # `_ws_reap_eval` calls this again on the normal path; it is idempotent.
  _ws_reap_reset

  # THE LOCK IS THE KERNEL'S, NOT A TRAP'S — and on this box that is the whole
  # argument. `mkdir` plus `trap … EXIT` was the shipped form, and a trap does
  # not run on SIGKILL: an OOM kill (this project's own speciality), a
  # `systemctl` hard stop, a power loss or a reboot each leave the directory
  # behind, every later `ws-reap` for that session answers `in-progress`, and
  # the RESUME PATH — the entire recovery mechanism — sits one refusal behind
  # it with no verb in ccd able to clear it. Measured, same fixture, only the
  # signal changed: SIGTERM left the lock free and the next run resumed;
  # SIGKILL left it HELD and every later run answered
  # `{"refused":"in-progress"}`, for ever. Step (i)'s `rm -f "$REG/$id".*` does
  # not match this name, and nothing else in the file does either.
  #
  # `flock` attaches an advisory lock to an OPEN FILE DESCRIPTION, and the
  # kernel drops it when the last copy of that description closes — which every
  # form of death does, including the ones no handler can see. Nothing has to
  # run for the lock to come back. Verified on this box (util-linux 2.39.3,
  # `flock from util-linux 2.39.3`): a second acquirer is refused while the
  # holder lives, and a `kill -9` of the holder frees it for the next acquirer.
  #
  # THE DESCRIPTION IS INHERITED BY CHILDREN, and that is the RIGHT semantics
  # here rather than a leak. Measured: a child of the holder keeps the lock
  # after the holder is SIGKILLed, and it is released when the child exits. The
  # case the old comment worried about — "an orphaned `git worktree remove`
  # grandchild keeps running" after the shell died — is exactly the case in
  # which a second reap must NOT start, and under a trap it was exactly the
  # case in which one could. Nothing in the destructive sequence daemonises
  # (`git worktree remove`, `systemctl --user disable --now`,
  # `tmux kill-session`, `rm -rf` are all short-lived clients), so the interval
  # is bounded by the work itself.
  #
  # THE LOCK FILE IS NEVER UNLINKED. Unlinking it while holding it is how two
  # processes each end up holding "the lock" on two different inodes: the
  # second `open()` after the unlink creates a NEW file, whose lock nobody
  # contends. What is left behind is a 0-byte hidden file per session that has
  # ever been offered to `ws-reap` — inert (the registry is read through
  # `$REG/*.workspace` and `$REG/$id.<field>`, and a dotfile matches neither),
  # and the price of a lock whose identity is an inode rather than a promise.
  # The BREADCRUMB remains the recovery record; this only serialises runs.
  local lock="$REG/.reap-$id.lock" lfd rc=0
  # NOT a degraded mode. Without `flock` the serialisation is absent, not
  # weaker, so the destructive verb does not run — the same shape as the
  # `_json_str` probe above, and the same `die`. Pinned by `refuses to run the
  # destructive verb unserialised when flock is missing`, which shims `command`
  # rather than emptying PATH, because every stub in that file spells its own
  # passthrough `command git`.
  command -v flock >/dev/null 2>&1 \
    || die "flock (util-linux) is unavailable — refusing to run the destructive verb unserialised"
  exec {lfd}>>"$lock" \
    || die "cannot open the reap lock at $lock"
  flock -n "$lfd" || {
    # Close OUR descriptor and touch nothing else: the winner's lock lives on
    # its own description and no path operation here can reach it. (Under the
    # mkdir form the loser's own trap could `rmdir` the winner's lock, which is
    # why that trap had to be armed after the mkdir rather than before it.)
    #
    # MUTATION SURVIVOR, disclosed and measured: this close is removable with
    # the whole suite green, because a refused caller is a caller that is about
    # to exit and the kernel closes it then. It is not the same line as the one
    # after `_ws_reap_locked`, which IS pinned (`gives the lock back when the
    # FUNCTION returns`): that one is on the path where the shell goes on to do
    # other things. This one stays so that "every path gives the descriptor
    # back" is a property of the function rather than of its callers.
    exec {lfd}>&-
    printf '{"refused":"in-progress","detail":%s,"paths":[]}\n' \
      "$(_json_str "another ccd process is already reaping $id and still holds the lock")"
    return 0
  }
  # EVERY return path gives the descriptor back, which is why the body is its
  # own function. `flock` treats two `open()`s of one path in one process as
  # two strangers, so a descriptor left open by one call refuses the NEXT call
  # in the same shell — and ccd is sourced (by `ccd` itself and by its tests),
  # so "the process exits eventually" is not the same statement as "the lock
  # went back".
  _ws_reap_locked "$token" "$id"; rc=$?
  exec {lfd}>&-
  return "$rc"
}

_ws_reap_locked() {   # token id — everything the reap lock serialises
  local token="$1" id="$2"
  local resumed; resumed=$(_reg_get "$id" reaping)
  if [[ -n "$resumed" ]]; then
    # Resume: the tombstone written at (b) is what distinguishes "the user
    # deleted the worktree" from "we did".
    #
    # `--expect` IS NOT CHECKED ON THIS PATH, and that is a decision rather than
    # an oversight, so it is written down here where the path forks. Everywhere
    # else the plan and the spec call the token THE consent boundary — "any
    # drift refuses `state-changed`" — and the argv still requires a shape-valid
    # 64-hex string, so `ws-reap` cannot be spelled without one. What it is not
    # is compared: there is nothing to compare it to. The token is
    # `_ws_reap_eval`'s, built from twelve facts Phase B and Phase C measured,
    # and on a resume the worktree is usually already gone — Phase B has no tree
    # to read and Phase C would need a gh call an outage could withhold for
    # ever, which is the wedge §5.6 exists to end. `cmd_ws_audit` says the same
    # thing from the other side by refusing to ISSUE a token for
    # `reap-interrupted`: a token nobody can obtain cannot be the boundary.
    #
    # What stands in its place is stricter in the ways that still have facts
    # behind them: the TOMBSTONE is the consent record — it exists only because
    # a token-carrying reap was authorised, and its `tip` is re-validated
    # against the live ref per phase below — and Phase B and Phase D1, the two
    # whose facts can still change in the gap, are re-proven in full. What is
    # accepted is that a SECOND human, holding any 64-hex string, can finish a
    # cleanup a first human authorised. Measured: after a kill at (c),
    # `ws-reap --expect ffff…ff` completed the reap.
    local tombtip; tombtip=$(sed -n 's/.*"tip"[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*"\([0-9a-f]*\)".*/\1/p' "$REG/.reaped/$id.json" 2>/dev/null | head -1)
    local branch; branch=$(_reg_get "$id" branch)
    # THE TIP IS REQUIRED ON EVERY PHASE. It is the CAS old-value at (g) and the
    # only proof this journal belongs to this branch, since Phase C is
    # deliberately not re-run here. Empty is the ABSENCE of that proof, never a
    # value: with the branch also gone the two empties compare equal, so the
    # emptiness test cannot be folded into the comparison below.
    if [[ -z "$tombtip" ]]; then
      printf '{"refused":"branch-moved","detail":%s,"paths":[]}\n' \
        "$(_json_str "no tombstone tip for $id — refusing to finish a cleanup whose journal cannot be read")"
      return 0
    fi
    # AND THE COMPARISON IS PER PHASE, because §5.6's "re-validate … THEN
    # continue from the recorded phase" is a contradiction once the phase is
    # `clips`: (g) has ALREADY CAS-deleted the branch by then, so `live` is
    # empty by construction and an unconditional comparison reads "moved" for
    # the one state in which gone is correct — permanently. Measured before it
    # was per phase: a kill at (h) answered `branch-moved` on every later
    # attempt, the clips directory leaked, the registry row survived with no
    # worktree and no branch, and the detail said "nothing was deleted after
    # the worktree" while everything up to and including the branch had been.
    #
    # `clips` is the ONLY phase that skips it, and the default arm re-validates:
    # a breadcrumb holding anything ccd did not write is not a phase this can
    # reason about, so it gets the stricter reading, not the looser one. What
    # protects (g) in the skipped case is (g)'s own compare-and-swap — a branch
    # recreated at another sha after the delete fails that CAS and refuses
    # there.
    case "$resumed" in
      clips) : ;;
      *)
        local live; live=$(git -C "$PROJECTS_ROOT/$(_reg_get "$id" project)" rev-parse --verify "refs/heads/$branch" 2>/dev/null)
        if [[ "$live" != "$tombtip" ]]; then
          printf '{"refused":"branch-moved","detail":%s,"paths":[]}\n' \
            "$(_json_str "the branch moved while cleaning up — nothing was deleted after the worktree")"
          return 0
        fi ;;
    esac

    # ── Phase B, AGAIN, on the resume path ────────────────────────────
    # §5.3 is unconditional: "every guard below is evaluated inside ws-reap, on
    # the box, at the instant of deletion". §5.6 authorises resuming a tail; it
    # does not authorise skipping the guards on the way through it. And the
    # breadcrumb is written at (c), BEFORE `git worktree remove` at (f), so
    # `reaping=worktree` WITH the worktree still on disk is the routine outcome
    # of one SIGTERM inside that window — not an exotic case. Without this
    # block the next reap deletes that worktree unaudited, and a .env written
    # between the two runs is gone with it.
    #
    # Phase C is deliberately NOT re-run: mergedness was proven before the
    # breadcrumb existed and the tombstone records the proof, and re-requiring
    # a gh read would let an outage strand a half-reaped workspace forever.
    # What is re-proven here is Phase B and Phase D1 — the guards whose facts
    # can still have changed in the gap, and the only two the resume can cost
    # anything by skipping.
    local workdir; workdir=$(_reg_get "$id" workdir)
    if [[ -d "$workdir" ]]; then
      # Both reads checked, for the reason spelled out at `_ws_reap_eval`'s Phase
      # B — and here it matters more, because this path has no token to fall back
      # on: nothing downstream compares a fingerprint, so an unreadable tree that
      # counted 0 dirty files and an unreadable ignored set that produced an empty
      # REAP_SENSITIVE would take `git worktree remove` straight through both
      # guards. `local x=$(cmd)` returns local's status, so the read is its own
      # statement.
      # AND STDERR IS CAPTURED, exactly as `_ws_reap_eval`'s Phase B captures
      # it (ccd:2109-2116) and for the same measured reason: a PARTIALLY
      # unreadable tree exits 0 with EMPTY stdout and `warning: could not open
      # directory 'sub/'` on stderr, so the count is 0, `dirty-tree` passes, and
      # the cleanup finishes over work it never saw. Two reads, one rule.
      #
      # TWO MUTATION SURVIVORS, disclosed and each measured whole-suite (44
      # files / 712 tests, exit 0): dropping the `&& [[ -z "$rerr" ]]` conjunct,
      # and restoring `2>/dev/null` so there is no `$rerr` to test. Both leave
      # the suite green, because `_ws_collect_ignored` two statements
      # below reads the same tree under the same rule and refuses
      # `tree-unreadable` first — measured with `chmod 000` on an untracked
      # directory holding uncommitted work: the resume DOES refuse and the work
      # DOES survive, but the refusal comes from the ignored read. This is
      # defence in depth, and it is written out because the ordering it relies
      # on is not a property anyone would preserve on purpose: reorder those two
      # statements, or relax the ignored read, and a partially unreadable tree
      # walks into `git worktree remove`.
      local rdirty rerrf rerr rrc
      rerrf=$(mktemp) || {
        printf '{"refused":"tree-unreadable","detail":%s,"paths":[]}\n' \
          "$(_json_str "could not read the tree at $workdir — refusing to finish the cleanup on a guess")"
        return 0
      }
      rdirty=$(git -C "$workdir" status --porcelain 2>"$rerrf"); rrc=$?
      rerr=$(cat "$rerrf" 2>/dev/null); rm -f "$rerrf"
      { (( rrc == 0 )) && [[ -z "$rerr" ]]; } || {
        printf '{"refused":"tree-unreadable","detail":%s,"paths":[]}\n' \
          "$(_json_str "could not read the tree at $workdir — refusing to finish the cleanup on a guess")"
        return 0
      }
      rdirty=$(printf '%s' "$rdirty" | grep -c . || true)
      if (( rdirty != 0 )); then
        printf '{"refused":"dirty-tree","detail":%s,"paths":[]}\n' \
          "$(_json_str "$rdirty uncommitted or untracked file(s) appeared while the cleanup was interrupted")"
        return 0
      fi
      # MUTATION SURVIVOR, disclosed: the `${REAP_IGNREASON:+ …}` here is
      # removable with the whole suite green — the EVALUATED site's identical
      # interpolation is pinned (by the scan-budget and unreadable-directory
      # fixtures, which both refuse before any breadcrumb exists), and no
      # fixture reaches a failing scan on the RESUME path, which needs a
      # breadcrumb AND a surviving worktree AND an unreadable ignored directory
      # at once. It stays because the two sites describe the same failure and
      # the remedy is the whole reason the reason exists.
      _ws_collect_ignored "$workdir" || {
        printf '{"refused":"tree-unreadable","detail":%s,"paths":[]}\n' \
          "$(_json_str "could not read the ignored set at $workdir${REAP_IGNREASON:+ — $REAP_IGNREASON} — refusing to finish the cleanup on a guess")"
        return 0
      }
      if (( ${#REAP_SENSITIVE[@]} != 0 )); then
        printf '{"refused":"sensitive-ignored","detail":%s,"paths":%s}\n' \
          "$(_json_str "${REAP_SENSITIVE[*]}")" "$(_reap_paths_json)"
        return 0
      fi

      # Phase D1 too, and for the same reason: the breadcrumb is written at (c),
      # BEFORE _ws_unsupervise at (d), so a SIGTERM in that window leaves
      # `reaping=worktree` with the session STILL RUNNING. Without this the
      # resume yanks the worktree out from under a live turn OR a running Bash
      # tool command — `idle` is an allowlist in _ws_status, so `shell` refuses
      # here (deviation 6). The tree is clean and pushed, so no bytes are lost,
      # but §5.3 is unconditional and session-busy is one of its guards.
      local rst; rst=$(_ws_status "$id") || {
        printf '{"refused":"status-unknown","detail":%s,"paths":[]}\n' \
          "$(_json_str "cannot read the wrapper status file — refusing to finish the cleanup on a guess")"
        return 0
      }
      if [[ "$rst" == busy ]]; then
        printf '{"refused":"session-busy","detail":%s,"paths":[]}\n' \
          "$(_json_str "the session is working — a model turn or a Bash tool command — and the cleanup was interrupted before it was stopped")"
        return 0
      fi
    fi

    REAP_TIP="$tombtip"
    _ws_reap_tail "$id" "$resumed"
    return 0
  fi

  if ! _ws_reap_eval "$id"; then
    local paths="[]"
    [[ "$REAP_VERDICT" == sensitive-ignored ]] && paths=$(_reap_paths_json)
    printf '{"refused":%s,"detail":%s,"paths":%s}\n' \
      "$(_json_str "$REAP_VERDICT")" "$(_json_str "$REAP_DETAIL")" "$paths"
    return 0
  fi

  # D2 — the consent IS the fingerprint, and it is checked HERE, in ccd. A
  # server-side check fails open into deletion; this one cannot.
  if [[ "$token" != "$REAP_TOKEN" ]]; then
    printf '{"refused":"state-changed","detail":%s,"paths":[]}\n' \
      "$(_json_str "expected $REAP_TOKEN, was given $token — this workspace changed since the list you were shown")"
    return 0
  fi

  _ws_reap_tail "$id" ""
}

_ws_reap_tail() {   # id resumed-phase — the journalled destructive sequence
  local id="$1" resumed="$2" project workdir branch main attic clips tomb bytes
  project=$(_reg_get "$id" project); workdir=$(_reg_get "$id" workdir); branch=$(_reg_get "$id" branch)
  main="$PROJECTS_ROOT/$project"
  bytes=$(_ws_gc_bytes "$workdir"); [[ "$bytes" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || bytes=0

  if [[ -z "$resumed" ]]; then
    attic=$(_ws_attic_pin "$main" "$id" "$workdir" "$REAP_TIP")            # (a)
    clips=$(_ws_clip_manifest "$id")
    tomb=$(_ws_tombstone "$id" "$clips")                                   # (b)
    _reg_set "$id" reaping worktree                                        # (c)
    _ws_unsupervise "$id"                                                  # (d)
    tmux kill-session -t "$(_tmux "$id")" 2>/dev/null || true              # (e)
  else
    # AND (d) AND (e) ARE NOT RE-RUN, which is safe only because of what stands
    # in front of this path: `_ws_reap_eval` refuses `not-archived` unless
    # `$REG/$id.archived` exists, and `cmd_ws_archive` (ccd:1063-1064) is what
    # writes it — after `_ws_unsupervise` and after `tmux kill-session`. So by
    # the time any breadcrumb can exist the unit is disabled and the pane is
    # gone, and re-running either would be a second call to an idempotent
    # no-op. Measured: a resumed reap completes with `unsup=0`. What it does NOT
    # cover is something re-supervising the session between the archive and the
    # reap; the resume's own Phase D1 re-proof refuses `session-busy` if that
    # something is actually working, which is the part that could cost bytes.
    tomb="$REG/.reaped/$id.json"
    attic=$(git -C "$main" for-each-ref --format='%(refname)' "refs/ccrc/attic/$id/" 2>/dev/null | grep -c . || true)
    # Pre-merge fix round, finding E: re-measure clips NOW, on the resume,
    # not whatever `_ws_clip_manifest` answered at the ORIGINAL (b) — this
    # run's (h), a few lines below, `rm -rf`s whatever is on disk at THIS
    # instant, and a clip pasted in the gap must not be destroyed with no
    # record of it anywhere. Before (h), same as everywhere else in this
    # function guards run immediately before the step they guard.
    clips=$(_ws_clip_manifest "$id")
    _ws_tombstone_reclip "$id" "$clips" || {
      printf '{"refused":"tombstone-unwritable","detail":%s,"paths":[]}\n' \
        "$(_json_str "could not update the tombstone's clips record for $id — refusing to finish the cleanup without an accurate record")"
      return 0
    }
  fi

  if [[ "$resumed" == "" || "$resumed" == worktree ]]; then
    if [[ -d "$workdir" ]]; then
      # No --force. On failure STOP: the session is already stopped and
      # ws-restore recovers it, whereas losing the registry would not be
      # recoverable.
      #
      # ONE invocation, with its stderr captured. Re-running the command just
      # to read its message can SUCCEED the second time — a lock released, a
      # file closed — and then this prints a refusal while the worktree is
      # actually gone and the breadcrumb still says `worktree`, which is a lie
      # in the one direction that matters.
      local wtout wtrc
      wtout=$(git -C "$main" worktree remove "$workdir" 2>&1); wtrc=$?
      if (( wtrc != 0 )); then
        printf '{"refused":"worktree-remove-failed","detail":%s,"paths":[]}\n' \
          "$(_json_str "$(printf '%s' "$wtout" | head -3)")"
        return 0
      fi
    fi
    _reg_set "$id" reaping branch
  fi

  # (g) Compare-and-swap, never `branch -d` (it refuses a squash merge and
  # succeeds when the branch merely equals its upstream) and never `-D`.
  #
  # The old-value operand is the whole mechanism, and it has TWO degenerate
  # values worth knowing about even though nothing here can reach either.
  # Measured on git 2.43: `update-ref -d <ref> 000…0` (40 zeros) and
  # `update-ref -d <ref> ""` BOTH delete unconditionally and exit 0, because git
  # reads each as "no old value given" rather than as a value to match — while
  # any other wrong sha exits 1 with `is at X but expected Y` and leaves the ref
  # alone. `$REAP_TIP` can be neither on either path: the evaluated one reads it
  # from `rev-parse --verify`, and the resume one takes it from the tombstone
  # only after `[[ -z "$tombtip" ]]` and an equality against a `rev-parse
  # --verify` of the live ref, which never answers zeros (an unresolvable ref
  # answers EMPTY, and empty != 000…0 refuses `branch-moved` above). Written
  # down because that is an argument about two other call sites, not about this
  # line, and the day either of them stops resolving the tip this degrades from
  # a compare-and-swap into an unconditional delete without failing anything.
  # The empty case is not hypothetical: deleting `REAP_TIP="$tombtip"` on the
  # resume path produced exactly it, and the suite stayed green until
  # `resumes against the tombstone tip, so the CAS is still a CAS` existed.
  #
  # THE `show-ref` GATE IS PINNED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, which took two fixtures
  # and is worth saying because one of them nearly was not written. `if false`
  # is killed by every test that reaps a live branch. `if true` — the SKIP
  # direction — survived the whole suite until `resumes from a clips
  # breadcrumb`: on that path the branch is already gone, so without the gate
  # `update-ref -d` runs against a ref that does not resolve, git exits 1, and
  # the run refuses `branch-moved` and leaves the registry row behind, which is
  # the F2 wedge manufactured on a path that would otherwise finish.
  if git -C "$main" show-ref --verify --quiet "refs/heads/$branch"; then
    git -C "$main" update-ref -d "refs/heads/$branch" "$REAP_TIP" 2>/dev/null || {
      printf '{"refused":"branch-moved","detail":%s,"paths":[]}\n' \
        "$(_json_str "the branch moved while cleaning up — nothing was deleted after the worktree")"
      return 0
    }
  fi
  _reg_set "$id" reaping clips

  # (h) Re-validate the id and assert the resolved path is a DIRECT CHILD of
  # ~/.cc-clips before any rm -rf.
  if [[ "$id" =~ ^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$ ]]; then
    # `>/dev/null` on every cd, and `--` before every operand: the house rule
    # ccrc/ws-rm-fix established at _ws_realpath and _ws_common_dir. Only `pwd -P`
    # may answer. Without the redirect a `cd` exported as a shell function
    # prepends its own print to $cdir (two cds, two lines) and to $croot (one cd,
    # one line), so the equality below fails and the clips directory silently
    # survives every reap. Without `--`, the regex above admits a leading hyphen,
    # so an id like `-P` would be read as cd's own option. Both failures are
    # fail-CLOSED — no rm runs — which is the right direction and still wrong.
    #
    # TWO MUTATION SURVIVORS, disclosed, and they are the two guards standing in
    # front of the only `rm -rf` in this file — so it is worth saying exactly why
    # neither can be reached rather than leaving that to be assumed. `cmd_ws_reap`
    # validated `$id` against this same regex at entry, so re-testing it here can
    # never change the answer; and for any id that PASSES the regex the child
    # assertion holds by arithmetic. The interesting case is `..`, which the
    # regex admits (`.` and `-` are both in the class) and which resolves to
    # $HOME, one level ABOVE the root — and the equality is what refuses it. It
    # is unreachable only because `_ws_reap_eval` refuses `..` far earlier, for
    # want of a `$REG/...uuid`. Both stay: a re-validation immediately before an
    # `rm -rf` is not redundancy, it is the last thing that runs before it.
    local cdir; cdir=$(cd -- "$HOME/.cc-clips" >/dev/null 2>&1 && cd -- "./$id" >/dev/null 2>&1 && pwd -P) || cdir=""
    local croot; croot=$(cd -- "$HOME/.cc-clips" >/dev/null 2>&1 && pwd -P) || croot=""
    [[ -n "$cdir" && -n "$croot" && "$cdir" == "$croot/$id" ]] && rm -rf "$cdir"
  fi

  rm -f "$REG/$id".*                                                       # (i) LAST
  # MUTATION SURVIVOR, disclosed: `${attic:-0}` is removable with the suite
  # green, because both arms above assign `attic` and neither can leave it
  # unset. It is `set -u` insurance on the ONE printf that reports a completed
  # deletion — an unbound variable here kills the process after the work is
  # done and before anything says so, which is the failure mode this whole
  # function is arranged to avoid.
  printf '{"reaped":%s,"branch":%s,"pr":%s,"proof":%s,"tombstone":%s,"attic":%s,"bytes":%s,"resumed":%s}\n' \
    "$(_json_str "$id")" "$(_json_str "$branch")" \
    "$( [[ "$REAP_PRNUM" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] && echo "$REAP_PRNUM" || echo null)" \
    "$(_json_str "$REAP_PROOF")" "$(_json_str "$tomb")" "${attic:-0}" "$bytes" \
    "$( [[ -n "$resumed" ]] && _json_str "$resumed" || echo null)"
}
```

`_ws_reap_tail` reads `REAP_*` globals that `_ws_reap_eval` set. On the resume
path only `REAP_TIP` is set (from the tombstone) — `REAP_PROOF`, `REAP_PRNUM`
and `REAP_MERGE` come back **empty, not unset**, which is why `cmd_ws_reap`
calls `_ws_reap_reset` before branching: empty is correct here (the resume
prints what it knows and the tombstone already recorded the rest), whereas
unset is fatal under `set -u`.

**Neither path in this task reads a branch name out of a directory, and that was
checked rather than assumed.** `cmd_ws_reap`'s resume arm and `_ws_reap_tail`
both take `branch` from `_reg_get "$id" branch` and then use it only against
`$main` — `rev-parse --verify "refs/heads/$branch"`, `show-ref --verify`,
`update-ref -d "refs/heads/$branch" "$REAP_TIP"`. There is no
`git -C "$workdir" rev-parse` anywhere in Task 6, so the unified read in Task 5
Step 4 is the whole change; the tail needs no edit. Two reasons that name is safe
by the time the tail runs: on the evaluated path `_ws_reap_eval` has already
refused unless git's worktree record corroborated it, and on **both** paths the
delete is a compare-and-swap against `$REAP_TIP`, so even a stale name can only
remove a ref that still points at the tip that was proven — `update-ref -d` with
an old-value operand fails rather than deleting, which is the `branch-moved`
refusal. What the CAS does *not* protect is a name that is wrong and current, and
the corroboration in Phase A is what rules that out.

```bash
git commit -m "feat(ccd): ws-reap — every guard on the box, at the instant of deletion

The prior shape had the refusals as client render decisions behind a
three-line DELETE route: a stale sheet, a second tab or one line of curl
removed all of them. Here it removes none. The --expect token is a
fingerprint of the state a human was shown, checked in ccd, and the
whitelist pins ['ws-reap','--expect'] so an unconfirmed reap cannot
cross the wire at all.

The attic goes first: git worktree remove deletes the per-worktree
reflog and deleting a branch deletes its own, so an amended-away commit
would become a dangling object with a two-week fuse and no name. Fifty
bytes a ref makes those commits referenced instead.

The branch is deleted by compare-and-swap, never branch -d (which
refuses a squash merge and succeeds on a branch that merely equals its
upstream) and never -D. A failed update-ref stops and refuses: an
orphaned branch is a bug, not an outcome. The breadcrumb is what makes
the tail resumable, and the lock is a flock the KERNEL releases when the
process dies — a trap does not run on SIGKILL, and a lock nothing can
release is a lock that hides the breadcrumb for ever."
```

### Task 7: `ws-gc` learns about archived and reaping workspaces

**Files:**
- Modify: `infra/<server-host>-portability/ccd:505-545` (`_ws_gc_row`),
  `:547-588` (`_ws_gc_scan`), `:601-653` (`_ws_gc_prune_row`),

- Modify (deviation 35 — required scope extension assigned by the Task 6

- Test: `infra/ccrc/server/test/ccd-ws-reap.test.ts`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: `$REG/<id>.archived`, `$REG/<id>.reaping` (Tasks 2 and 6).
- Produces: a new `archived` row state; `--prune` declines it; dead-reg
  reclamation skips archived and reaping ids; `.reaped/` is never touched.
- Produces (deviation 35): a new refusal token, `reaping-phase-unknown`, from
  `_ws_reap_tail` — see Task 13's `SENTENCES` table.

**Context.** `ws-gc --prune`'s `dead-reg` arm runs `rm -f "$REG/$id".*`, which
would delete an archived workspace's registry — the only thing that knows where
its worktree and branch are — and would delete a mid-reap breadcrumb, turning a
resumable tail into an orphan. `.reaped/` is a directory, so it cannot match
`*.workspace`, but the scan asserts it anyway.

`_ws_reap_tail`'s worktree-removal step was gated by the LOOSE test
`[[ "$resumed" == "" || "$resumed" == worktree ]]`: a breadcrumb holding ANY
other value — including one ccd never writes — falls to the ELSE of that

breadcrumb of `reaping=sometime-else` with the worktree still on disk finished

orphaned worktree, still registered with git, standing next to a deleted
branch, on a run that claimed success. `_ws_reap_locked`'s tip re-validation
already treats an unrecognised phase the STRICT way for the same uncertainty
(`case "$resumed" in clips) : ;; *) <re-validate> ;; esac`); this applies the
same rule to the tail's own dispatch.

In `_ws_reap_tail`, immediately after the `bytes=` line and before the
`if [[ -z "$resumed" ]]` block:

```bash
  # A breadcrumb holding anything ccd did not write is not a phase this can
  # reason about, so it gets the stricter reading, not the looser one — the
  # same rule `_ws_reap_locked`'s tip re-validation already states for the same
  # uncertainty. The LOOSE reading used to live below, as
  # `[[ "$resumed" == "" || "$resumed" == worktree ]]`: an unrecognised value is
  # neither `""` nor `worktree`, so it fell to the ELSE of that single test —
  # `git worktree remove` silently skipped — and the run then fell straight
  # through to (g)'s branch delete, (h)'s clips delete and (i)'s registry
  # delete, and reported `{"reaped":...}`. Measured: a breadcrumb of
  # `reaping=sometime-else` with the worktree still on disk finished with
  # `wt-exists true`, the branch gone, and the registry gone — an orphaned
  # worktree, still registered with git, standing next to a deleted branch,
  # on a run that claimed success. Checked BEFORE any of (f)/(g)/(h)/(i).
  case "$resumed" in
    ""|worktree|branch|clips) : ;;
    *)
      printf '{"refused":"reaping-phase-unknown","detail":%s,"paths":[]}\n' \
        "$(_json_str "breadcrumb phase '$resumed' for $id is not one ccd ever writes — refusing to guess which steps already ran")"
      return 0 ;;
  esac
```

New refusal token: `reaping-phase-unknown`. Recorded here for Task 13, whose
`SENTENCES` table (`ccd:11876` in this plan's draft) now carries it.

Two tests added to `infra/ccrc/server/test/ccd-ws-reap.test.ts`'s `describe('partial
failure and resume', ...)` block: `resumes from a branch breadcrumb — worktree

### Task 8: Retire `ws-rm` from ccrc — the unguarded door closes

**Files:**
- Modify: `infra/ccrc/server/src/server.ts:313-316` (delete the route)
- Modify: `infra/ccrc/pwa/src/lib/api.ts:121` (delete `workspaceRemove`)
- Modify: `infra/ccrc/pwa/src/fleet/SessionActionsSheet.tsx:35`, `:65-79`, `:103-112`
- Test: `infra/ccrc/server/test/workspaces-route.test.ts`,
  `infra/ccrc/pwa/test/session-actions-sheet.test.tsx`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: nothing.
- Produces: `DELETE /api/sessions/:id/workspace` no longer exists (404);
  `api.workspaceRemove` no longer exists. Task 17 adds the guarded replacement
  at the same tap target.

**Context.** `SessionActionsSheet:65-67` says *"No confirm dialog: ccd ws-rm
refuses a dirty tree, an unmerged branch and a main checkout, and says why."*
**That comment is false on the middle clause**, and that is the reason this task
exists: `ws-rm` does not refuse an unmerged branch. It keeps it and *warns* —
`git -C "$main" branch -d "$branch" 2>/dev/null || echo "kept branch … delete it
with: git -C $main branch -D …" >&2` (`ccd:386-389`) — and a warning on the
stderr of a background `exec` is not something a PWA tap has anywhere to put.

**Re-verified against `20d8829`, because the `ccrc/ws-rm-fix` merge rewrote
`cmd_ws_rm` and retired the sharpest version of this argument.** The plan used to
say `ws-rm` "swallows `branch -d`'s failure with `2>/dev/null || true` and orphans
the branch". **It no longer does**, and that sentence must not be repeated
anywhere: the merge replaced the swallow with the warning above, reads the branch
from git's worktree record (`_ws_wt_branch`) so the name survives the directory
being deleted, refuses a directory that is not a worktree of `$main` before any
teardown, refuses a `git status` it could not read, and declines to delete a
branch name the registry asserts but git never corroborated. Silent orphaning is
fixed. Say so.

What survives the merge, and is the whole case for this task:

- **Its only data guard is still `git status --porcelain`** (`ccd:355-358`), which
  cannot see gitignored content. A worktree holding `SECRET_API_KEY=…` in `.env` is
  deleted today with the output `removed workspace …` and nothing else. No
  manifest, no sensitive-ignored refusal, nothing on screen.
- **It still checks nothing about the remote.** No stash count, no
  unpushed-commits check, no fetch, no question asked of GitHub — so it cannot
  know whether the work it is deleting is in `main`, and it does not claim to.
- **It still has no confirmation and no fingerprint**, so nothing re-proves the
  world at the instant of deletion. It is a one-tap irreversible action whose
  guard evaluated whenever the pane last rendered.

Those three are untouched by the merge and are not fixable by tightening `ws-rm`:
they are what `ws-audit` → confirm → `ws-reap` exists to provide. Which is why the
verb is retired *from ccrc* here rather than deleted from `ccd` — a terminal user
who wants the sharp tool still has it, with a better warning than before.

This lands **before** the whitelist change (Task 9) deliberately: with nothing
emitting `ws-rm`, removing its grant is a no-op rather than a window in which a
live route answers `forbidden`. It also lands before the guarded replacement

### Task 9: The exec whitelist becomes argv-prefix matching, with no `gh` key

**Files:**
- Modify: `infra/ccrc/agent/src/whitelist.ts:93-126`
- Modify: `infra/ccrc/agent/test/whitelist.test.ts:117-129`
- Test: **Create** `infra/ccrc/agent/test/whitelist-noghosts.test.ts`
- Modify: `infra/ccrc/agent/test/exec.test.ts`, `infra/ccrc/agent/test/malformed.test.ts`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: nothing.
- Produces: `isExecAllowed(cmd: string, args: string[]): boolean` — unchanged
  signature, prefix semantics. `EXEC_WHITELIST` stays module-private, so the
  type change is not an API change.

**Context.** Prefixes pin a *leading run* of tokens; tokens after the prefix
are unconstrained. That is why **every new verb takes `--flag value` pairs only
with no free positionals** — putting a flag after a variable `<id>` positional
would make it unpinnable, and that is exactly how a `--body-file <any path>` or
a `--drop-ignored` becomes whitelist-legal. `['ws-reap','--expect']` is a
machine-checked statement that ccrc cannot reap without a token.

The `whitelist.isExecAllowed` describe block (`whitelist.test.ts:93-150`) holds
**7** `it`s — 14 is every `it` in the file, including the `canonicalize` and
`checkPath` blocks, which this change does not touch. All 7 pass unmodified
except the one asserting `ws-rm` is allowed (`:126-129`), which inverts. There
is **no assertion that `clip` is allowed** anywhere in that file, so nothing
inverts for it: `clip`'s removal is a silent grant deletion, and the only thing
that notices is Task 11's layer 3 (a grant no route builds) and
`whitelist-noghosts.test.ts`. That is worth knowing before the run — otherwise
a `clip` assertion gets hunted for and eventually invented.

```ts
// This file exists to FAIL LOUDLY if a `gh` key is ever added to
// EXEC_WHITELIST, and to pin the two verbs that were removed from it.
//
// The host's gh token carries the `repo` WRITE scope (gh auth status: gist,
// read:org, repo, workflow) and there is no second layer — no read-only
// credential, no cwd sandbox. Any `gh` entry makes this list the sole control
// between the PWA and `gh pr merge`. `gh: [['api']]` is strictly worse still:
// -X POST|PATCH|PUT creates, closes and merges PRs. Every PR read and the one
// PR write go through `ccd` verbs, whose args[0] has no write sibling
// reachable by changing args[1].
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { isExecAllowed } from '../src/whitelist.js';

describe('there is no gh key, in any form', () => {
  it.each([
    ['pr', 'view', '1'], ['pr', 'list'], ['pr', 'create'], ['pr', 'merge', '1'],
    ['pr', 'close', '1'], ['pr', 'edit', '1'], ['pr', 'ready', '1'], ['pr', 'comment', '1'],
    ['api', 'repos/o/r/pulls'], ['api', '-X', 'POST', 'repos/o/r/pulls'],
    ['repo', 'delete', 'o/r'], ['auth', 'token'], ['auth', 'status'],
  ])('refuses gh %s %s', (...args) => {

      .toBe(false);
  });

  it('refuses gh with no arguments at all', () => {
    expect(isExecAllowed('gh', [])).toBe(false);
  });

  it('refuses git outright, including a force push', () => {
    expect(isExecAllowed('git', ['push', '--force'])).toBe(false);
    expect(isExecAllowed('git', ['status'])).toBe(false);
  });
});

describe('the removed grants stay removed', () => {
  it('refuses ws-rm — the unguarded legacy verb', () => {
    // Its only data guard is `git status --porcelain`, which cannot see a
    // gitignored .env; it asks the remote nothing; and it carries no
    // confirmation to re-prove the tree at the instant of deletion.

  it('refuses clip — a dead grant with no server call site', () => {
    expect(isExecAllowed('ccd', ['clip', '/tmp/x.png'])).toBe(false);

  it('refuses ws-gc in every form — ["ws-gc"] would permit --prune', () => {
    expect(isExecAllowed('ccd', ['ws-gc'])).toBe(false);
    expect(isExecAllowed('ccd', ['ws-gc', '--prune'])).toBe(false);

    expect(isExecAllowed('ccd', ['ws-reap', '--expect', 'a'.repeat(64), '--session', 'x'])).toBe(true);
    expect(isExecAllowed('ccd', ['ws-reap', 'x'])).toBe(false);
    expect(isExecAllowed('ccd', ['ws-reap'])).toBe(false);
    expect(isExecAllowed('ccd', ['ws-reap', '--session', 'x'])).toBe(false);
    expect(isExecAllowed('ccd', ['ws-reap', '--session', 'x', '--expect', 'a'.repeat(64)])).toBe(false);
  });
});

describe('prefix matching is a prefix, not a substring', () => {
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Replace the whitelist**

Replace `infra/ccrc/agent/src/whitelist.ts:93-126` in full with:

```ts
/** cmd -> allowed argv PREFIXES. `args` must begin with one of them; tokens
 *  after the prefix are unconstrained. One-token prefixes are exactly the old
 *  behaviour, so every pre-existing entry is bit-identical. */
const EXEC_WHITELIST: Record<string, readonly (readonly string[])[]> = {
  tmux: [['has-session'], ['list-panes'], ['capture-pane'], ['send-keys'], ['resize-window']],

  // NO `gh` KEY, DELIBERATELY. The host token carries the `repo` WRITE scope
  // (gh auth status: gist, read:org, repo, workflow) and there is no second
  // layer — no read-only credential, no cwd sandbox. Any `gh` entry makes this
  // list the sole control between the PWA and `gh pr merge`. `gh: [['api']]` is
  // strictly worse still: -X POST|PATCH|PUT creates, closes and merges PRs.
  // PR reads and the one PR write go through `ccd` verbs, whose args[0] has no
  // write sibling reachable by changing args[1]. See whitelist-noghosts.test.ts.
  //
  // `ws-rm` is GONE from this list: it is the unguarded legacy verb and the PWA
  // must not be able to emit it. `ws-reap` replaces it and is pinned to carry
  // `--expect`, so an UNCONFIRMED reap cannot cross the wire at all.
  // `clip` is GONE: dead grant, no server call site emits it.
  // `ws-gc` is absent and must stay absent: ['ws-gc'] would permit `--prune`.
  ccd: [
    ['start'], ['enable'], ['ensure'], ['stop'], ['swap'], ['ws-add'],
    ['pr-state', '--session'],
    ['pr-state', '--project'],
    ['pr-open',  '--session'],
    ['ws-archive', '--session'],
    ['ws-restore', '--session'],
    ['ws-audit', '--session'],
    ['ws-reap',  '--expect'],   // load-bearing: no reap without a confirmation token
    ['ws-attic', '--session'],
  ],
};

export function isExecAllowed(cmd: string, args: string[]): boolean {
  if (typeof cmd !== 'string' || cmd.length === 0 || cmd.includes('/')) return false;
  const prefixes = EXEC_WHITELIST[cmd];
  if (!prefixes) return false;
  if (!Array.isArray(args) || !args.every((a) => typeof a === 'string')) return false;
  return prefixes.some((p) => p.length <= args.length && p.every((tok, i) => args[i] === tok));
}
```

Keep the existing doc comment above `isExecAllowed` (`whitelist.ts:107-118`)
about exact bare-command matching — it is still exactly true.

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: `ccd caps` (Task 2).

  - `AgentReady { t: 'ready'; v: 1; ccdVerbs?: string[] }`
  - `FleetState { connected: boolean; downSince: number | null; ccdVerbs: string[] | null }`
    — declared **once**, in `fleetstate.ts`, re-exported by `remote/client.ts`
  - `timeoutMsFor(cmd: string, args: string[]): number` (module-private in
    `runner.ts`, exercised through `createRunner`)
  - agent `MAX_EXEC_TIMEOUT_MS = 300_000`

**Context.** `~/.local/bin/ccd` is a **copy**, not a symlink to the repo, so a
verb can pass the whitelist and still not exist on the box — the class of
failure the `ws-add`/`ws-rm` defect belongs to, where every suite is green and
the control is dead on the fleet. The agent reads `ccd caps` once at start and
reports it; the server refuses to emit a verb the agent did not advertise and
renders `unsupported` instead of a control that silently fails.

`ws-reap` on a 4.8 G worktree would be SIGTERM'd mid-delete at the agent's
current 120 s ceiling, which is precisely the "killed mid-flight" row in the
error table — so the ceiling rises in the same change that introduces the
per-verb timeouts, not after it.

```ts
const CCD_TIMEOUT_MS = 90_000;
const TMUX_TIMEOUT_MS = 10_000;
// Give the round trip some slack over the agent's own exec timeout so a
// legitimately slow-but-finishing command doesn't get raced by our local
// per-request wait timeout.
const CLIENT_TIMEOUT_SLACK_MS = 5_000;

/** Per-verb budgets. `pr-state` shells out to gh over the network; `ws-reap`
 *  can be deleting several gigabytes of node_modules. The flat 90 s was fine
 *  while every ccd call was a tmux/systemd operation and is wrong for both
 *  ends of that range now. `pr-open` is deliberately absent, but NOT because
 *  ccd bounds it: its gh calls carry `timeout 12` and its `git push` — the
 *  likeliest thing in the verb to hang — carries no bound of its own. The flat
 *  CCD_TIMEOUT_MS default is what bounds the push, and 90 s is the right budget
 *  for one, so there is nothing to override here. */
const CCD_VERB_TIMEOUT_MS: Record<string, number> = {
  'pr-state': 20_000,
  'ws-archive': 60_000,
  'ws-restore': 60_000,
  // Equals CCD_TIMEOUT_MS's own default below — kept explicit, as
  // documentation that ws-audit's budget was chosen deliberately (a fleet
  // scan over every workspace) and not just left to fall through unnoticed,
  // even though no test can tell this line apart from its own absence.
  'ws-audit': 90_000,
  'ws-reap': 240_000,
};

function timeoutMsFor(cmd: string, args: string[]): number {
  if (cmd !== 'ccd') return TMUX_TIMEOUT_MS;
  // `?? ''` guards an empty `args` (args[0] === undefined) from reaching the
  // lookup as a literal `undefined` key. Provably redundant against THIS
  // map, disclosed rather than removed: no key here is `''` or the coerced
  // `"undefined"`, so an empty-array lookup misses either way and the `??
  // CCD_TIMEOUT_MS` below already covers the miss — the guard would only
  // change behaviour if a future verb were ever keyed `''`.
  return CCD_VERB_TIMEOUT_MS[args[0] ?? ''] ?? CCD_TIMEOUT_MS;
}
```
